name: Acne and spots
summary: Acne is very common, especially in teenagers, and causes spots on the face, back and chest. Mild acne can be treated with pharmacy products, and effective treatments are available from a doctor.
redFlags: A spreading, hot, red, painful area of skin with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A painful, swollen, hot spot or lump that is spreading
Severe acne with fever and joint pain

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Puberty, periods, pregnancy and polycystic ovary syndrome increase oil production.

commonCauses.title: Blocked hair follicles
commonCauses.detail: Oil and dead skin block pores and bacteria cause inflammation.

commonCauses.title: Family history
commonCauses.detail: Acne often runs in families.

commonCauses.title: Cosmetics and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Oily make-up and some medicines can trigger spots.

selfCare: Wash affected areas twice a day with a mild cleanser and lukewarm water
Use non-comedogenic (non-pore-blocking) make-up and moisturisers
Ask a pharmacist about creams or gels containing benzoyl peroxide
Give treatments 2 to 3 months to work
avoid: Squeezing or picking spots, which can cause scarring
Washing more than twice a day or scrubbing hard
Unproven remedies such as toothpaste on spots
seeDoctorIf: Pharmacy treatments have not helped after 2 to 3 months
You have painful, deep spots or lumps (nodules or cysts)
Acne is leaving scars or dark marks
Acne is affecting your confidence or mood

name: Allergic reaction
summary: Mild allergic reactions cause itching, sneezing or a rash. A severe reaction (anaphylaxis) affects breathing or circulation and is a medical emergency: call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112).
redFlags: Swelling of the lips, tongue, mouth or throat
Difficulty breathing, wheezing, a hoarse voice or a tight throat
Feeling faint, dizzy, confused or collapsing
Pale, cold or blue-tinged skin, or a fast, weak pulse
Severe reaction after a sting, food or medicine in someone with a known severe allergy
urgentFlags: Swelling of the face or eyes without breathing problems
A widespread itchy rash after a new medicine
Symptoms that are getting worse despite antihistamines

commonCauses.title: Foods
commonCauses.detail: Peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish and sesame are common triggers.

commonCauses.title: Insect stings
commonCauses.detail: Bee and wasp stings.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Antibiotics such as penicillin, anti-inflammatory painkillers and others.

commonCauses.title: Latex, pollen, pets or dust mites
commonCauses.detail: Usually cause milder reactions such as hay fever symptoms or hives.

selfCare: If you have an adrenaline auto-injector, use it at the first signs of a severe reaction and call your local emergency number
Lie down with legs raised if feeling faint, or sit up if struggling to breathe
For mild reactions, ask a pharmacist about antihistamines
Avoid the trigger once identified
avoid: Waiting to see if a severe reaction gets better
Standing up or walking during a severe reaction, even if you feel better
Unproven allergy tests such as hair analysis or applied kinesiology
seeDoctorIf: You have had an allergic reaction and do not know the cause
You have had a severe reaction and do not have an allergy plan or auto-injector
Mild symptoms keep coming back

name: Anger or irritability
summary: Anger is a normal emotion, but frequent irritability or outbursts that are hard to control can affect relationships and wellbeing. It is often linked to stress, tiredness, low mood or anxiety.
redFlags: You feel you might seriously hurt yourself or someone else
Someone is in immediate danger from violence
Sudden personality change or aggression with confusion, headache or weakness
urgentFlags: Anger leading to hurting people or damaging things
Irritability with very little sleep, racing thoughts and unusually high energy
Thoughts of suicide or self-harm

commonCauses.title: Stress and tiredness
commonCauses.detail: Pressure and poor sleep make it harder to manage emotions.

commonCauses.title: Depression or anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Both can show up as irritability.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Can lower self-control and worsen anger.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Premenstrual changes and menopause can affect mood.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Trauma can make anger more likely.

selfCare: Notice early signs such as a racing heart or clenched fists, and step away
Take slow breaths and count to 10 before responding
Exercise to release tension
Talk it through later when calm
Look into anger management courses or self-help programmes
avoid: Drinking alcohol or using drugs when angry
Driving when very angry
Bottling anger up until it explodes
seeDoctorIf: Anger is affecting your relationships, work or daily life
You feel irritable most of the time
You are worried about how you behave when angry

name: Anxiety or constant worry
summary: Everyone feels anxious sometimes, but anxiety that is strong, hard to control or lasts a long time can affect daily life. It is common and there are effective ways to manage and treat it.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, or feeling you might act on them
Chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint that you are not sure is anxiety
You feel you are in immediate danger or cannot keep yourself safe
urgentFlags: Anxiety so severe you cannot carry out daily tasks or leave the house
Thoughts of self-harm or suicide without a plan to act on them
Using alcohol or drugs to cope and feeling out of control

commonCauses.title: Stressful life events
commonCauses.detail: Work, money, relationships, health worries or big changes can trigger anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
commonCauses.detail: Ongoing, excessive worry about many things that is hard to control.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Difficult or traumatic experiences can make anxiety more likely.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine, alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Stimulants and withdrawal can cause or worsen anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Physical health conditions
commonCauses.detail: An overactive thyroid and some medicines can cause anxiety-like symptoms.

selfCare: Try slow breathing: breathe in gently through your nose and out slowly through your mouth
Be physically active most days
Talk to someone you trust about how you feel
Try evidence-based self-help such as online cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) resources
Keep regular sleep, cut down on caffeine and alcohol
avoid: Using alcohol, drugs or smoking to cope
Avoiding situations that make you anxious, which can make anxiety worse over time
Unregulated supplements marketed as anxiety cures
seeDoctorIf: Anxiety is affecting your daily life or causing you distress
Self-help has not helped after a few weeks
You have physical symptoms such as palpitations that worry you
You think you may have an anxiety disorder or panic attacks

name: Baby crying non-stop
summary: All babies cry, and colic, wind and tiredness are common reasons. Crying that sounds different, or comes with a fever or your baby being unwell, needs to be checked.
redFlags: A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry that is not like their normal cry
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
Difficulty breathing, blue or grey lips, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Green vomit, or blood in their poo
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it, or a bulging soft spot on the head
urgentFlags: Crying with not feeding, or vomiting most feeds
Crying with a high temperature
Fewer wet nappies than usual
Crying that seems to come with pain, such as drawing up the legs repeatedly with paleness
A swelling in the groin or a swollen, red scrotum

commonCauses.title: Hunger, tiredness or a dirty nappy
commonCauses.detail: The most common reasons for crying.

commonCauses.title: Colic
commonCauses.detail: Long periods of crying, often in the evening, in an otherwise healthy baby; usually starts in the first few weeks and improves by 3 to 4 months.

commonCauses.title: Wind or reflux
commonCauses.detail: Discomfort during or after feeds.

commonCauses.title: Illness
commonCauses.detail: Infections, ear pain or, rarely, a twisted bowel or hernia.

selfCare: Check if your baby is hungry, tired, too hot or too cold, or needs a nappy change
Hold your baby close, rock or walk gently, and try white noise or a warm bath
Wind your baby during and after feeds
If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby safely on their back in their cot and take a few minutes to calm down
Ask your health visitor, midwife or doctor for support
avoid: Ever shaking a baby; this can cause serious brain injury
Changing formula repeatedly without advice
Unproven colic remedies, herbal teas or giving water to young babies
seeDoctorIf: Your baby cries a lot and you are struggling to cope
Your baby is not gaining weight or feeding well
Crying has not improved by 4 months
You think your baby might have reflux or a cow's milk allergy

name: Baby floppy, drowsy or not feeding
summary: A baby who is unusually floppy, very drowsy or not feeding can be seriously ill, even without a high temperature. Trust your instincts and get help quickly.
redFlags: Floppy, unresponsive, or very hard to wake
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
Difficulty breathing, grunting, pauses in breathing, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
A seizure (fit), or a bulging soft spot on the head
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months, or a temperature below 36C (96.8F)
urgentFlags: Feeding much less than usual or refusing feeds
Fewer wet nappies than usual, or no wet nappy for 8 hours or more
Vomiting most feeds
Yellow skin or eyes with sleepiness and poor feeding
Your baby is just not themselves and you are worried

commonCauses.title: Infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds and viruses can reduce feeding; serious infections such as sepsis or meningitis must be ruled out.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration
commonCauses.detail: From vomiting, diarrhoea or poor feeding.

commonCauses.title: Jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Newborns with jaundice can be sleepy and feed poorly.

commonCauses.title: Feeding difficulties
commonCauses.detail: Problems with latch or positioning, or a blocked nose.

selfCare: Get medical help straight away if any warning signs are present
Keep offering feeds little and often
Count wet nappies and note when your baby last fed
Ask a midwife, health visitor or doctor for feeding support
avoid: Waiting overnight to see if a floppy or very drowsy baby improves
Giving water or other drinks instead of milk to young babies
seeDoctorIf: Your baby is not gaining weight
Feeding is often difficult or painful
You are worried about your baby's feeding or sleep

name: Back pain
summary: Back pain is very common and usually improves within a few weeks. Staying active is one of the best things you can do.
redFlags: Numbness or tingling around the genitals or bottom
Difficulty peeing, being unable to pee, or losing control of your bladder or bowels
Weakness or numbness in both legs, or being unsteady on your feet
Back pain with chest pain, or sudden severe back pain with fainting
Back pain after a serious fall or accident
urgentFlags: Back pain with a high temperature or feeling unwell
Back pain with numbness, weakness or pins and needles in one leg that is getting worse
Pain that is getting worse quickly, or is severe at night or at rest
Back pain with unexplained weight loss, or a history of cancer
Swelling or a change in the shape of your back

commonCauses.title: Muscle or ligament strain
commonCauses.detail: Often after lifting, twisting or awkward movement; the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Sciatica
commonCauses.detail: Pain shooting down the leg from an irritated nerve in the lower back.

commonCauses.title: Wear and tear
commonCauses.detail: Age-related changes in the spine, which are very common and often cause no pain.

commonCauses.title: Posture and inactivity
commonCauses.detail: Long periods sitting or poor working positions.

commonCauses.title: Kidney infection or other causes
commonCauses.detail: Pain in the side or back with a high temperature can come from the kidneys.

selfCare: Keep moving and continue normal activities as much as you can
Take ibuprofen or paracetamol, following the pack instructions
Use heat packs or cold packs to ease pain
Try gentle back stretches and exercise such as walking, swimming or yoga
Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees
avoid: Bed rest for more than a day or two
Heavy lifting until pain eases
Sitting for long periods without moving
seeDoctorIf: Pain has not improved after a few weeks
Pain stops you doing day-to-day activities
Pain is very bad or getting worse over time
You are worried about the pain or struggling to cope

name: Bad breath
summary: Bad breath is common and usually caused by bacteria in the mouth, especially when teeth, gums and tongue are not cleaned well. It can usually be treated at home.
redFlags: Fruity-smelling breath with vomiting, stomach pain, fast breathing or confusion, especially in someone with diabetes
urgentFlags: Bad breath with a painful swollen gum or face and a high temperature
Bad breath with a painful, ulcerated mouth and fever

commonCauses.title: Oral hygiene
commonCauses.detail: Food and bacteria build up on the teeth, gums and tongue.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease or tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Infections in the mouth often cause a bad smell.

commonCauses.title: Strong foods, smoking and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Garlic, onions, coffee, tobacco and alcohol affect breath.

commonCauses.title: Dry mouth
commonCauses.detail: Less saliva lets bacteria build up.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Sinus or throat infections, acid reflux and some health conditions can cause bad breath.

selfCare: Brush teeth and gums twice a day for 2 minutes
Clean between your teeth daily and gently clean your tongue
Keep dentures clean and take them out at night
Drink water and chew sugar-free gum
Stop smoking
avoid: Relying on mouthwash or mints to hide the smell
Sugary snacks and drinks
Strong-smelling foods before social events if they affect you
seeDoctorIf: Bad breath does not go away after a few weeks of good cleaning
You have painful, bleeding or swollen gums
You have toothache or loose adult teeth
You have problems with your dentures

name: Barking cough in a child (croup)
summary: Croup is a common viral illness in young children that causes a barking cough, a hoarse voice and noisy breathing. Most cases are mild and get better within 48 hours, but some children need treatment.
redFlags: Your child is struggling to breathe, or the skin is sucking in under the ribs or at the neck
Blue, grey or very pale lips or skin
Your child is unusually drowsy, floppy, quiet or not responding
Your child is drooling, cannot swallow, or is leaning forward to breathe
Your child stops breathing for a moment
urgentFlags: A harsh, high-pitched noise when breathing in (stridor) even when calm or resting
Symptoms that are getting worse
A high temperature or your child seems very unwell
Your child is restless or agitated, or not drinking

commonCauses.title: Viral croup
commonCauses.detail: Caused by viruses such as parainfluenza; most common between 6 months and 3 years.

commonCauses.title: Spasmodic croup
commonCauses.detail: Sudden barking cough at night that can come back.

commonCauses.title: Other causes of noisy breathing
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, an inhaled object or a serious throat infection.

selfCare: Keep your child calm and sit them upright; crying can make symptoms worse
Give plenty of fluids
Use children's paracetamol or ibuprofen for a high temperature or discomfort, following the pack instructions for their age
Check on your child regularly during the night
avoid: Putting your child in a steamy room or using steam, which is not proven to help and can cause scalds
Cough medicines for young children
Smoking around your child
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not improved after 2 days
Your child keeps getting croup
You are worried about your child's breathing

name: Black or very dark poo
summary: Iron tablets, bismuth stomach medicines and some foods can turn poo black. Black, sticky, tar-like poo can also mean bleeding in the stomach and must be checked quickly.
redFlags: Black, sticky, tar-like poo with dizziness, fainting, a fast heartbeat or cold, clammy skin
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black poo with severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black, sticky or tar-like poo that is not explained by iron tablets, bismuth medicines or food
Black poo with stomach pain or indigestion
Black poo while taking blood thinners or anti-inflammatory painkillers

commonCauses.title: Iron tablets or bismuth medicines
commonCauses.detail: These commonly turn poo dark green or black and are harmless in that case.

commonCauses.title: Foods
commonCauses.detail: Black liquorice, blueberries and beetroot can darken poo.

commonCauses.title: Bleeding in the stomach or upper bowel
commonCauses.detail: A stomach ulcer or inflamed stomach lining can bleed, giving sticky, tar-like black poo.

selfCare: Check whether you have recently started iron tablets, bismuth medicines or eaten dark foods
If none of these explain it, get medical advice the same day
Keep a note of any medicines you take, including painkillers, to tell the doctor
avoid: Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin until you have been checked
Waiting to see if unexplained black, sticky poo goes away
Alcohol until you have been checked
seeDoctorIf: Your poo stays dark and you are unsure why
You feel tired and look pale
You have ongoing indigestion or stomach pain

name: Bleeding after the menopause
summary: Any vaginal bleeding a year or more after your last period is not normal and should be checked by a doctor. It is often caused by something treatable, but it can be an early sign of womb cancer.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting or a racing heart
urgentFlags: Heavy or continuous bleeding
Bleeding with pelvic pain and a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Thinning of the vaginal or womb lining
commonCauses.detail: Lower oestrogen after the menopause can make the tissues thin and bleed easily.

commonCauses.title: Hormone replacement therapy
commonCauses.detail: HRT can cause some bleeding, especially when starting or changing treatment.

commonCauses.title: Polyps
commonCauses.detail: Small non-cancerous growths in the womb or cervix.

commonCauses.title: Thickened womb lining or womb cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason any bleeding after the menopause must be investigated.

selfCare: Make an appointment with a doctor even if the bleeding was light or happened once
Note when the bleeding happened and how heavy it was
avoid: Waiting to see if it happens again
Assuming it is a period returning
seeDoctorIf: You have any bleeding a year or more after your last period
You have unexpected bleeding while on HRT
You have new vaginal discharge after the menopause

name: Bleeding between periods or after sex
summary: Light spotting can happen with hormonal contraception or around ovulation, but bleeding between periods or after sex should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting or a racing heart
Bleeding with severe tummy pain if you could be pregnant
urgentFlags: Bleeding with a positive pregnancy test
Bleeding with a high temperature, pelvic pain or unusual smelly discharge

commonCauses.title: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.detail: Spotting is common when starting or changing pills, implants, injections or hormonal coils, or after missing pills.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea can cause bleeding after sex or between periods.

commonCauses.title: Cervical changes or polyps
commonCauses.detail: Small growths or changes on the cervix can bleed, especially after sex.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Bleeding can happen in early pregnancy, including with miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Cervical or womb cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason unexplained bleeding should be checked.

selfCare: Do a pregnancy test if you could be pregnant
Keep a diary of when bleeding happens
Make sure you are up to date with cervical screening
avoid: Ignoring bleeding after sex
Assuming spotting is caused by contraception without checking if it continues
seeDoctorIf: You have bleeding between periods or after sex
Spotting on contraception lasts more than 3 months
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You are 45 or over with new irregular bleeding

name: Bleeding from the bottom
summary: Bright red blood on toilet paper is often caused by piles or a small tear, but blood in your poo should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Bleeding that is heavy or will not stop
Large amounts of blood or blood clots in the toilet
Bleeding with dizziness, fainting, a fast heartbeat or cold, clammy skin
Black, sticky, tar-like poo with feeling faint or unwell
Bleeding with severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black or dark red poo
Bloody diarrhoea, especially with a high temperature
Bleeding that has lasted more than a day or two
Bleeding in a child

commonCauses.title: Piles (haemorrhoids)
commonCauses.detail: Bright red blood after pooing, sometimes with itching or a lump around the bottom.

commonCauses.title: Anal fissure
commonCauses.detail: A small tear in the skin of the bottom, causing sharp pain when pooing and bright red blood.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Some stomach bugs cause bloody diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis can cause blood and mucus with diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Bowel polyps or cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason any blood in poo should be checked, especially if you are older or your bowel habits have changed.

selfCare: Eat more fibre and drink plenty of fluids to keep poo soft
Do not strain on the toilet
Gently pat the area clean with moist toilet paper
Ask a pharmacist about creams for piles if that is the likely cause, while waiting to see a doctor
avoid: Assuming bleeding is piles without being checked
Pushing or straining when pooing
Ignoring bleeding because it has stopped
seeDoctorIf: You have any blood in your poo, even once, that has not been checked
You have a change in bowel habits lasting 3 weeks or more
You have lost weight without trying or feel very tired
You have a lump in or around your bottom

name: Bleeding or pain in early pregnancy
summary: Light bleeding in early pregnancy is fairly common and does not always mean a problem, but it should always be checked, as it can be a sign of miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy.
redFlags: Sharp, sudden or severe pain in your tummy, especially on one side
Pain in the tip of your shoulder
Dizziness, fainting or feeling very unwell
Heavy bleeding, soaking through pads, or passing large clots
Pain when pooing or peeing with bleeding and feeling faint
urgentFlags: Any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy
Cramping pain in the lower tummy
Bleeding or pain after a positive pregnancy test when you have not yet had a scan
A gush of fluid from the vagina

commonCauses.title: Implantation bleeding or cervical changes
commonCauses.detail: Light spotting can happen early in pregnancy or after sex because the cervix is more sensitive.

commonCauses.title: Miscarriage
commonCauses.detail: Bleeding with cramping in the first 23 weeks; sadly common, especially in the first 12 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Ectopic pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: The pregnancy grows outside the womb, usually in a tube; it can cause one-sided pain, bleeding and shoulder-tip pain and is an emergency.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Vaginal or cervical infections can cause light bleeding.

selfCare: Contact your midwife, doctor or an early pregnancy unit the same day
Use pads rather than tampons so the amount of bleeding can be judged
Rest while you wait to be seen
avoid: Waiting at home with severe pain or heavy bleeding
Using tampons while bleeding in pregnancy
Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen in pregnancy unless advised
seeDoctorIf: You had bleeding that has stopped but you have not yet been checked
You have had a previous ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage and are pregnant again

name: Bleeding or swollen gums
summary: Gums that bleed when you brush are most often a sign of gum disease (gingivitis), which is common and can be reversed with good cleaning. A dentist can check and treat it.
redFlags: Bleeding that will not stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Very swollen gums with swelling spreading to the face or neck and difficulty swallowing or breathing
urgentFlags: Very sore and swollen gums
Teeth becoming loose or falling out
Bleeding gums with unexplained bruising, nosebleeds or feeling very tired
Painful, ulcerated gums with bad breath and fever

commonCauses.title: Gingivitis
commonCauses.detail: Plaque build-up along the gumline causing red, swollen gums that bleed.

commonCauses.title: Brushing too hard or flossing for the first time
commonCauses.detail: Can cause minor bleeding that settles.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Hormone changes make gums more likely to bleed.

commonCauses.title: Periodontitis
commonCauses.detail: More advanced gum disease that can loosen teeth.

commonCauses.title: Medicines or blood conditions
commonCauses.detail: Blood thinners or, rarely, blood disorders can cause bleeding gums.

selfCare: Brush twice a day for 2 minutes with a fluoride toothpaste and a soft brush
Clean between your teeth every day with floss or interdental brushes
Keep brushing gums that bleed; bleeding usually improves within 1 to 2 weeks
Stop smoking
Have regular dental check-ups and cleaning
avoid: Stopping brushing because your gums bleed
Brushing very hard with a hard brush
Sugary snacks and drinks between meals
seeDoctorIf: Your gums bleed when you brush or eat hard foods
Your gums are painful and swollen
You have bad breath that does not go away
You have not had a dental check-up for 2 years

name: Blisters
summary: Blisters are small pockets of fluid, usually caused by friction, burns or sunburn. Most heal on their own within a week.
redFlags: Widespread blistering or skin peeling in sheets, especially after starting a new medicine
Blisters in the mouth, eyes or genitals with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A blister that looks infected: hot, swollen, very painful, or filled with yellow or green pus
Blisters from a burn that are larger than your hand
Blisters that keep appearing for no clear reason
Blisters on the feet if you have diabetes

commonCauses.title: Friction
commonCauses.detail: From shoes, tools or exercise.

commonCauses.title: Burns and sunburn
commonCauses.detail: Heat, chemicals or too much sun.

commonCauses.title: Skin conditions or infections
commonCauses.detail: Eczema, chickenpox, shingles, impetigo or allergic reactions.

selfCare: Leave the blister to heal on its own if possible
Cover it with a soft plaster or padded dressing
If it bursts, wash the area, leave the loose skin in place and cover it
Wear comfortable, well-fitting shoes and moisture-wicking socks
avoid: Popping or peeling a blister
Wearing the shoes or doing the activity that caused it until healed
seeDoctorIf: A blister has not healed after a week
You keep getting blisters with no clear cause
You have blisters in unusual places, such as the eyelids or mouth

name: Bloating
summary: Bloating is when your stomach feels full, tight or swollen. It is usually caused by wind or diet and often eases on its own.
redFlags: A swollen stomach with severe pain and being unable to pass poo or wind
Bloating with vomiting that will not stop
Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
urgentFlags: A stomach that is swollen and getting bigger quickly
Bloating with a high temperature or feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Wind and diet
commonCauses.detail: Beans, onions, fizzy drinks and swallowing air can all cause bloating.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: Hard or infrequent poo often comes with bloating.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Bloating that comes and goes with cramps and changes in bowel habit.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance
commonCauses.detail: For example lactose (milk sugar) or wheat intolerance.

commonCauses.title: Ovarian problems
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, bloating that is there most days can be a sign of ovarian cancer.

selfCare: Exercise regularly to help your bowel move
Eat smaller meals and eat slowly
Cut down on fizzy drinks, chewing gum and foods that give you wind
Keep a food diary to spot triggers
Ask a pharmacist about remedies for wind or constipation
avoid: Cutting out whole food groups without advice
Unproven 'detox' teas and supplements
seeDoctorIf: You have been bloated most days for 3 weeks or more
You have bloating that keeps coming back
You also have weight loss, blood in your poo or a change in bowel habit
You are over 50 and have new, persistent bloating

name: Blocked ear or ear wax
summary: A blocked feeling in the ear is often caused by earwax, a cold, or pressure changes when flying. It usually clears on its own or with simple treatment.
redFlags: Blocked ear with sudden face drooping, weakness or slurred speech
Blocked ear after a head injury with fluid coming out
urgentFlags: Sudden hearing loss not explained by a cold or wax
Severe ear pain, high temperature or discharge
Something stuck in the ear

commonCauses.title: Earwax build-up
commonCauses.detail: Wax can build up and cause muffled hearing, itching or ringing.

commonCauses.title: Colds and sinus congestion
commonCauses.detail: Swelling blocks the tube between the ear and the back of the nose.

commonCauses.title: Pressure changes
commonCauses.detail: Flying, diving or driving in mountains can cause a blocked, popping ear.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or glue ear
commonCauses.detail: Fluid in the middle ear causes fullness and reduced hearing.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about ear drops or olive oil drops to soften wax, if your eardrum is not damaged
Lie with the affected ear upwards for a few minutes after putting drops in
Swallow, yawn or chew gum to help an ear pop after flying
Gently breathe out with your mouth closed while pinching your nose to clear pressure
avoid: Using cotton buds, fingers or objects to clean inside the ear
Ear candles, which do not work and can cause burns
Using ear drops if you have had a perforated eardrum or ear surgery, unless advised
seeDoctorIf: Earwax symptoms have not cleared after 5 days of drops
Your ear is badly blocked and you cannot hear
You keep getting blocked ears

name: Blocked or stuffy nose
summary: A blocked nose is usually caused by a cold, hay fever or sinusitis and gets better on its own. A nose blocked on one side only for weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Swelling around the eyes with fever, vision changes or difficulty moving the eye
A blocked nose with a severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or a rash that does not fade
Difficulty breathing (not just a blocked nose)
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell or getting worse despite self-care
Severe pain in the face or forehead that painkillers do not help
You have a weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Common cold
commonCauses.detail: Viral infection with a blocked or runny nose that improves within 1 to 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever, dust mites or pets can cause a blocked, itchy, sneezy nose.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed sinuses causing a blocked nose, facial pain and reduced smell.

commonCauses.title: Nasal polyps or a deviated septum
commonCauses.detail: Can cause long-term blockage, often worse on one side.

selfCare: Rinse your nose with a saltwater (saline) spray or rinse
Breathe in steam, for example in a warm shower
Raise your head with an extra pillow at night
Ask a pharmacist about decongestants or antihistamines that suit you
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
avoid: Using decongestant nasal sprays for more than about a week, as they can make congestion worse
Smoking and smoky rooms
Antibiotics for a cold, which do not work against viruses
seeDoctorIf: Your blocked nose has lasted more than 3 weeks
It is only ever blocked on one side
You have nosebleeds or bloody discharge with it
You keep getting sinusitis

name: Blood in urine
summary: Blood in your pee can be caused by an infection or kidney stones, but it can also be a sign of something more serious, so it should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Being unable to pee at all
Passing large blood clots or heavy bleeding
Feeling faint, confused or very unwell with a high or very low temperature
urgentFlags: Blood in your pee with pain in your back or side
Blood in your pee with a high temperature or shivering
Blood in your pee after an injury
Passing small blood clots

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Often with burning, needing to pee often and cloudy pee.

commonCauses.title: Kidney stones
commonCauses.detail: Usually with severe pain in the side, back or groin that comes in waves.

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Can cause blood in the pee in older men.

commonCauses.title: Kidney or bladder disease or cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason blood in pee always needs tests.

commonCauses.title: Harmless colour changes
commonCauses.detail: Beetroot, blackberries, some medicines and periods can colour pee red or pink.

selfCare: Think about whether food such as beetroot, a medicine, or a period could explain the colour
Drink enough fluids so your pee is pale
Book a doctor's appointment even if it only happened once
avoid: Ignoring blood in your pee because it has stopped
Taking leftover antibiotics without advice
seeDoctorIf: You have seen blood in your pee, even once
A urine test has found blood
You have a need to pee more often or a weak flow

name: Blue or grey lips or skin
summary: Lips, tongue or skin that turn blue, grey or very pale can mean the body is not getting enough oxygen. When it comes on suddenly it is an emergency.
redFlags: Lips, tongue or skin suddenly turning blue, grey or very pale (on brown or black skin, check the palms, gums or around the eyes)
Blue lips with difficulty breathing or choking
Blue lips with confusion, drowsiness or collapse
A child who is blue, limp or not responding normally
urgentFlags: Fingers or toes that stay blue or white after warming up
Bluish lips that come and go with exercise

commonCauses.title: Cold
commonCauses.detail: Fingers, toes and lips can look blue in the cold and improve with warming.

commonCauses.title: Breathing problems
commonCauses.detail: Severe asthma, pneumonia, COPD or choking reduce oxygen levels.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Heart failure or heart conditions present from birth.

commonCauses.title: Raynaud's phenomenon
commonCauses.detail: Fingers and toes turn white then blue in the cold or with stress.

selfCare: If someone suddenly turns blue or grey and is struggling to breathe, call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112)
If only fingers and toes are blue from cold, warm up gradually
avoid: Waiting to see if blue lips improve when someone is breathless or unwell
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: Your fingers or toes often change colour in the cold
Lips or nails look bluish with exercise or breathlessness

sources.label: MedlinePlus – Blue discoloration of the skin

name: Blurred vision
summary: Blurred vision often comes on gradually and is commonly due to needing glasses, tired or dry eyes, or cataracts. Sudden blurred vision, especially with other symptoms, needs urgent care.
redFlags: Sudden blurred vision or loss of vision in one or both eyes
Blurred vision with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Blurred vision with a severe headache, or a red, painful eye and feeling sick
Blurred vision after an eye or head injury
urgentFlags: New blurred vision with flashing lights, floaters or a shadow across vision
Blurred vision with eye pain or sensitivity to light
Blurred or double vision that has come on over a few days
Blurred vision with very high blood sugar readings or during pregnancy with headache or swelling

commonCauses.title: Needing glasses or a change of prescription
commonCauses.detail: Short-sightedness, long-sightedness and age-related focusing changes are very common.

commonCauses.title: Dry or tired eyes
commonCauses.detail: Screen use and dry eyes can make vision blur on and off.

commonCauses.title: Cataracts
commonCauses.detail: Gradual cloudy or misty vision, glare and halos, mostly in older adults.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes and other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Changing blood sugar, macular degeneration and glaucoma can affect vision.

selfCare: Have a sight test with an optician
Take regular breaks from screens: every 20 minutes, look at something far away
Use lubricating eye drops from a pharmacy if your eyes feel dry
Do not drive if your vision is not clear
avoid: Driving while your vision is blurred
Ignoring sudden changes in vision
Buying reading glasses instead of having a full eye test if vision has changed
seeDoctorIf: Your vision has been gradually getting blurry
You have not had a sight test in the last 2 years
You have diabetes and notice changes in your vision
Blurring keeps coming back

name: Brain fog or poor concentration
summary: Brain fog describes feeling slow, foggy or unable to concentrate. It is commonly linked to tiredness, stress, low mood, poor sleep or recovering from an illness.
redFlags: Sudden confusion or difficulty thinking that came on over minutes or hours
Difficulty thinking with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Drowsiness or confusion after a head injury
urgentFlags: Thinking is getting noticeably worse over days
Brain fog with a high temperature, severe headache or being sick
Brain fog after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Tiredness and poor sleep
commonCauses.detail: Not getting enough good-quality sleep affects concentration and memory.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or depression
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain often shows up as difficulty concentrating.

commonCauses.title: After an infection
commonCauses.detail: Many people feel foggy for a while after viral illnesses, including COVID-19.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal and other health changes
commonCauses.detail: Menopause, an underactive thyroid, anaemia and some medicines can cause brain fog.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and aim for enough sleep
Break tasks into smaller steps and take regular breaks
Do some gentle physical activity most days
Eat regular balanced meals and drink enough water
Cut down on alcohol
avoid: Relying on energy drinks or lots of caffeine
Supplements that claim to boost brain power, which have little evidence
seeDoctorIf: Brain fog has lasted more than a few weeks
It is affecting your work or daily life
You also feel very tired, low or have other symptoms such as weight change

name: Breast lump or change
summary: Most breast lumps are not cancer, but any new lump or change in the breast, nipple or armpit should be checked by a doctor. This applies to men too.
redFlags: A red, hot, painful breast with a high temperature and feeling very unwell, confused or faint
urgentFlags: A red, hot, swollen and painful area of the breast, especially when breastfeeding
A painful lump with a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Cysts
commonCauses.detail: Fluid-filled sacs that can feel smooth and may be tender, often around periods.

commonCauses.title: Fibroadenoma
commonCauses.detail: A smooth, rubbery, movable lump, common in younger women.

commonCauses.title: Mastitis or abscess
commonCauses.detail: Painful, hot, red breast, usually when breastfeeding.

commonCauses.title: Breast cancer
commonCauses.detail: Can cause a lump, skin dimpling, a nipple change or discharge, or a lump in the armpit.

selfCare: Get to know how your breasts normally look and feel
Book an appointment for any new lump or change, even if painless
Attend breast screening when invited
avoid: Waiting until after your next period to see if a lump goes away if you are worried
Assuming a painless lump is harmless
seeDoctorIf: You find a new lump or thickening in the breast or armpit
Your breast changes size or shape, or the skin dimples or puckers
You have nipple discharge, a rash on the nipple or a nipple that turns inwards
You are a man with a breast lump

name: Breast pain
summary: Breast pain is common, often linked to periods, pregnancy or a poorly fitting bra, and is rarely a sign of cancer on its own.
redFlags: Chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with breathlessness or sweating
A red, hot, painful breast with feeling very unwell, confused or faint
urgentFlags: A red, hot, swollen area of the breast, especially when breastfeeding
Breast pain with a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Pain in both breasts in the days before a period, during pregnancy or when starting hormonal medicines.

commonCauses.title: Bra fit or exercise
commonCauses.detail: A poorly fitting bra or lack of support during activity.

commonCauses.title: Breastfeeding problems
commonCauses.detail: Blocked ducts, mastitis or sore nipples.

commonCauses.title: Chest wall pain
commonCauses.detail: Muscle strain or inflammation of the rib joints can feel like breast pain.

selfCare: Wear a well-fitting, supportive bra, including a sports bra for exercise and a soft bra at night
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Keep a diary to see if pain is linked to your periods
If breastfeeding, keep feeding or expressing and ask a midwife or health visitor about positioning
avoid: Stopping breastfeeding suddenly if you have a blocked duct or mastitis
Supplements such as evening primrose oil, which have little evidence of benefit
seeDoctorIf: Pain is not linked to your periods and has lasted more than a few weeks
Pain is in one specific area
You also have a lump, nipple discharge or skin changes
Pain is affecting your daily life

name: Bruising easily
summary: Bruising more easily is common with age and with some medicines. Unexplained bruising, especially with other symptoms, should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Tiny red or purple spots or bruises that do not fade when pressed, with a high temperature or feeling very unwell
Bruising with bleeding that will not stop
A bruise after a head injury with drowsiness, confusion or vomiting
Bruising with vomiting blood or black poo
urgentFlags: Lots of unexplained bruises or tiny red-purple spots appearing
Bruising with nosebleeds or bleeding gums
Bruising while taking blood thinners
Unexplained bruises on a child or a vulnerable adult

commonCauses.title: Ageing skin
commonCauses.detail: Skin and blood vessels become thinner, so bruises appear with minor knocks.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Blood thinners, aspirin, anti-inflammatory painkillers and long-term steroids increase bruising.

commonCauses.title: Unnoticed knocks
commonCauses.detail: Many bruises come from bumps you do not remember.

commonCauses.title: Blood or clotting disorders
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, low platelets, liver disease or blood cancers.

selfCare: Use a cold pack wrapped in a towel on a new bruise
Rest and raise the bruised area if you can
Make a list of all medicines and supplements you take to show the doctor
avoid: Stopping a prescribed blood thinner without talking to your doctor
Supplements that can affect bleeding, such as high-dose fish oil or ginkgo, without advice
seeDoctorIf: You bruise easily for no obvious reason
You have large or frequent bruises
You also feel very tired, have night sweats or weight loss
A bruise has not improved after 4 weeks

name: Burn or scald
summary: Small, minor burns can be treated at home after cooling them under running water. Larger, deep or chemical burns, and burns in young children, need medical care.
redFlags: A large or deep burn, bigger than the injured person's hand
A burn that is white, charred or leathery, or has no pain
Burns to the face, hands, feet, genitals, or across a joint, that are more than minor
Chemical or electrical burns
Breathing difficulty, a hoarse voice or soot around the mouth or nose after a fire
A burn in someone who is confused, very drowsy or in shock
urgentFlags: Any burn with blisters in a child under 5 or a pregnant person
A burn that looks infected: increasing pain, redness, swelling or pus
A burn in someone with diabetes or a weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Hot liquids and steam
commonCauses.detail: Scalds from drinks, kettles and baths are the most common burns in children.

commonCauses.title: Hot surfaces and flames
commonCauses.detail: Cookers, irons, hair straighteners and fires.

commonCauses.title: Chemicals and electricity
commonCauses.detail: These can cause deeper damage than they appear.

selfCare: Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible
Remove clothing or jewellery near the burn unless stuck to the skin
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
Keep the person warm, while cooling the burn
avoid: Ice, iced water, butter, toothpaste or creams on the burn
Popping blisters
Sticky or fluffy dressings that may stick to the burn
seeDoctorIf: A burn has not healed within 2 weeks
A minor burn is very painful or you are unsure how bad it is
You are unsure if your tetanus vaccination is up to date

name: Calf pain or swelling in one leg
summary: Calf pain is often a muscle strain or cramp, but pain with swelling and warmth in one leg can be a blood clot (DVT), which needs same-day assessment.
redFlags: Calf pain or swelling with sudden breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood
A cold, pale, numb or very painful leg
urgentFlags: Throbbing or cramping pain with swelling in one leg, usually the calf or thigh
Warm, red or darkened skin over the painful area
Calf pain after recent surgery, a long journey, a period of immobility, or during pregnancy or after birth
Swollen veins that are hard or sore when touched

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain or cramp
commonCauses.detail: Pain after exercise or a sudden movement, without major swelling.

commonCauses.title: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
commonCauses.detail: A blood clot in a deep vein; risk is higher after surgery, long journeys, in pregnancy, or with some contraceptive pills.

commonCauses.title: Baker's cyst
commonCauses.detail: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee that can burst and cause calf pain.

commonCauses.title: Poor circulation
commonCauses.detail: Cramping pain when walking that eases with rest, more common in smokers.

selfCare: If a clot is possible, get medical advice the same day before doing anything else
For a clear muscle strain, rest, apply a cold pack and raise the leg
Paracetamol can ease pain, following the pack instructions
avoid: Massaging a calf that might have a blood clot
Ignoring one-sided calf swelling
seeDoctorIf: Calf pain has not improved after 2 weeks
You get pain in your calves when walking that eases when you stop
Calf pain keeps coming back

name: Can't sleep (insomnia)
summary: Insomnia means regularly having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early. It is common, often linked to stress, and usually improves by changing sleep habits.
redFlags: Not sleeping with thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Going days without sleep with racing thoughts, very high energy, or seeing or hearing things others do not
urgentFlags: Severe distress or inability to function because of lack of sleep
Sleep problems after starting or stopping a medicine, with feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and depression
commonCauses.detail: Worry and low mood are among the most common causes.

commonCauses.title: Sleep habits and environment
commonCauses.detail: Irregular hours, screens, a noisy or bright bedroom and naps.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine, alcohol and nicotine
commonCauses.detail: These disrupt sleep, especially later in the day.

commonCauses.title: Shift work and jet lag
commonCauses.detail: Disrupt the body clock.

commonCauses.title: Health problems
commonCauses.detail: Pain, needing to pee at night, menopause, sleep apnoea, restless legs and some medicines.

selfCare: Go to bed and get up at the same times every day
Keep your bedroom dark, quiet and cool
Avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening, and limit alcohol
Wind down before bed and keep screens out of bed
If you cannot sleep, get up and do something calm, then return to bed when sleepy
Be physically active during the day, but not just before bed
avoid: Long daytime naps
Using alcohol to help you sleep
Relying on over-the-counter sleeping pills for more than a few nights
seeDoctorIf: Changing your sleep habits has not helped
You have had trouble sleeping for months
Insomnia is affecting your daily life
You snore loudly, stop breathing in your sleep or have restless legs

name: Catarrh or mucus in the throat
summary: Catarrh is a build-up of mucus in the nose, sinuses and back of the throat. It usually follows a cold or comes with allergies and clears up on its own.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing
Swelling around the eyes with fever or vision changes
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell with a high temperature
Blood-stained mucus from one side of the nose

commonCauses.title: Colds and sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Infections make the lining of the nose produce more mucus.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and dust or pet allergies can cause ongoing mucus.

commonCauses.title: Non-allergic rhinitis
commonCauses.detail: A long-term runny or blocked nose without an allergy.

commonCauses.title: Nasal polyps
commonCauses.detail: Soft growths that can cause long-term catarrh and reduced smell.

selfCare: Rinse your nose with salt water
Drink plenty of fluids and get enough rest
Keep the air moist and avoid very warm, dry rooms
Sleep with your head slightly raised
avoid: Things that trigger symptoms, such as smoke or known allergens
Dairy-free diets to clear mucus, which have no good evidence
Overusing decongestant sprays
seeDoctorIf: Catarrh lasts more than a few weeks
You develop new symptoms such as a sore throat, problems swallowing or loss of smell
It is affecting your sleep or daily life

name: Change in bowel habits
summary: A change in how often you poo or what it looks like that lasts for weeks is worth getting checked. Most causes are not serious, but it can be an early sign of bowel cancer.
redFlags: Heavy bleeding from the bottom
Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Black, sticky, tar-like poo
Bloody diarrhoea with a high temperature
Feeling very unwell with ongoing diarrhoea

commonCauses.title: Diet or lifestyle changes
commonCauses.detail: Changes in food, fluids, activity or stress can alter bowel habits for a while.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Diarrhoea, constipation or both, with cramps and bloating that come and go.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: New medicines can cause constipation or diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Ongoing diarrhoea, weight loss or blood and mucus need tests.

commonCauses.title: Bowel cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason a persistent change, especially with blood or weight loss, should be checked.

selfCare: Keep a diary of your bowel habits, diet and any symptoms to show the doctor
Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fibre and drink enough fluids
Take part in bowel cancer screening when invited
avoid: Waiting months to see if a persistent change settles
Self-treating with laxatives or anti-diarrhoea medicines for weeks without advice
seeDoctorIf: A change in bowel habits has lasted 3 weeks or more
You have blood in your poo
You have lost weight without trying
You have a lump in your stomach or bottom, or feel very tired for no reason

name: Changing or new mole
summary: Most moles are harmless, but a new mole or one that changes in size, shape or colour should be checked, as it can be an early sign of melanoma skin cancer.
redFlags: A mole or skin spot that is bleeding heavily and will not stop
urgentFlags: A mole that is growing quickly
A mole that has started bleeding, crusting or oozing

commonCauses.title: Normal mole changes
commonCauses.detail: Moles can change slowly over many years, especially in younger people and during pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Seborrhoeic keratosis
commonCauses.detail: Harmless, warty brown 'stuck-on' spots that become more common with age.

commonCauses.title: Melanoma
commonCauses.detail: A mole with an uneven shape or border, several colours, a size over 6mm, or that is changing.

commonCauses.title: Other skin cancers
commonCauses.detail: A shiny lump, a sore that does not heal or a scaly patch on sun-exposed skin.

selfCare: Check your skin every month, using a mirror or asking someone to help
Take photos to compare changes over time
Protect your skin from the sun: shade, clothing, sunscreen of SPF 30 or more, and no sunbeds
avoid: Using sunbeds
Trying to remove a mole yourself, including with creams sold online
Relying on apps alone to decide whether a mole is safe
seeDoctorIf: A mole changes size, shape or colour
A mole has an uneven border or more than 2 colours
A mole is itchy, crusty, bleeds or looks inflamed
You notice a new mole as an adult that looks different from your other moles
You have a sore that has not healed within 4 weeks

name: Chest pain or tightness
aliases: pain in left side of chest
summary: Chest pain has many causes and is often not caused by the heart, but it can be a sign of a heart attack. Sudden chest pain or pressure that does not go away needs emergency help.
redFlags: Sudden pain, pressure, squeezing or tightness in the chest that does not go away
Chest pain that spreads to the arms, neck, jaw, stomach or back
Chest pain with sweating, feeling sick, light-headed or short of breath
Sudden sharp chest pain with breathlessness or coughing up blood
Chest pain lasting 15 minutes or more
urgentFlags: Sharp chest pain that comes and goes, or only happens when breathing or coughing
Chest pain on exertion that eases with rest
Chest pain with a high temperature and cough

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Pain after exercise, lifting or injury, worse when pressing the area or moving.

commonCauses.title: Heartburn or indigestion
commonCauses.detail: Burning pain after eating, often with a sour taste.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety or panic attack
commonCauses.detail: Sharp or tight pain with a racing heart, sweating and dizziness.

commonCauses.title: Chest infection or pleurisy
commonCauses.detail: Pain often worse on breathing in or coughing.

commonCauses.title: Heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Angina or a heart attack; pain often feels like pressure, heaviness or tightness.

selfCare: If you think it could be a heart attack, call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112), sit down and rest while waiting
If a pharmacist or doctor has said it is muscle pain, use heat and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol, following the pack instructions
If heartburn is likely, ask a pharmacist about remedies and avoid large late meals
avoid: Driving yourself to hospital with chest pain
Assuming chest pain is indigestion without getting it checked
Exercising until chest pain has been assessed
seeDoctorIf: You have chest pain that comes and goes
You had chest pain that went away quickly but you are still worried
You get chest pain or tightness when walking or climbing stairs

name: Chills and shivering
summary: Shivering and feeling cold are often the body's way of raising its temperature at the start of an infection. Uncontrollable shaking with feeling very unwell can be a sign of sepsis.
redFlags: Shivering uncontrollably with feeling very unwell, confused or very drowsy
Cold, blotchy, pale or blue-tinged skin, lips or tongue
Fast breathing, breathlessness or a very fast heartbeat
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
Not peeing all day
Very low body temperature after being outside in the cold, with confusion or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Shivering with pain when peeing or pain in your back or side
Shivering with a red, hot, swollen area of skin
Shivering with a weakened immune system, such as during chemotherapy
Chills after travel abroad

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Flu and other viruses often cause chills along with a high temperature.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infection
commonCauses.detail: Kidney, chest or skin infections can cause severe shivering (rigors).

commonCauses.title: Cold exposure
commonCauses.detail: Being cold or wet for a long time.

commonCauses.title: Malaria
commonCauses.detail: Chills and fever after visiting an area with malaria, even months later.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use a light blanket while shivering, and remove extra layers once you feel hot
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen if you feel unwell, following the pack instructions
Check your temperature and other symptoms regularly
avoid: Piling on lots of blankets if you have a high temperature
Hot baths when feeling faint or very unwell
seeDoctorIf: Chills keep coming back
You have had chills and a temperature for more than 3 days
You also have night sweats or weight loss

name: Chipped, broken or knocked-out tooth
summary: A chipped, cracked or knocked-out tooth needs to be seen by a dentist. An adult tooth that has been knocked out has the best chance of being saved if it is put back or kept moist and seen within an hour.
redFlags: Head injury with the dental injury, such as being knocked out, vomiting or confusion
Bleeding from the mouth that will not stop after 15 minutes of pressure
Jaw that may be broken, or cannot close the mouth properly
Swelling making it difficult to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: An adult tooth has been knocked out
A tooth is badly broken, loose or pushed out of place
Severe pain or a broken tooth with exposed pink or red inner part

commonCauses.title: Falls and sports injuries
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause of knocked-out or broken front teeth.

commonCauses.title: Biting hard objects
commonCauses.detail: Ice, hard sweets, bones or pen tops can crack teeth.

commonCauses.title: Tooth decay or large fillings
commonCauses.detail: Weakened teeth break more easily.

commonCauses.title: Teeth grinding
commonCauses.detail: Can crack teeth over time.

selfCare: Hold a knocked-out adult tooth by the crown (white part), not the root
If it is dirty, rinse it briefly in milk or saliva, then push it back into the socket and bite on a clean cloth
If you cannot put it back, keep it in milk or in your cheek and see a dentist straight away
For a chipped tooth, keep any pieces, rinse your mouth and see a dentist
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Putting a knocked-out baby tooth back in, as it can damage the adult tooth underneath
Scrubbing the tooth or storing it in water
Chewing on the broken tooth
seeDoctorIf: A tooth feels sensitive or has changed colour after an injury
A small chip has left a sharp edge
A filling or crown has come out

name: Cold sores
summary: Cold sores are small blisters on or around the lips caused by the herpes simplex virus. They are common and usually clear up on their own within 10 days.
redFlags: Cold sore near the eye with eye pain, redness or changes in vision
A newborn baby with blisters or who is unwell after contact with a cold sore
Widespread sores with high fever, confusion or drowsiness
urgentFlags: A cold sore near or in the eye
Swollen, painful gums and many sores inside the mouth, especially in a child
Cold sores with a weakened immune system or eczema around the sore

commonCauses.title: Herpes simplex virus
commonCauses.detail: Once you have the virus it stays in the body and can reactivate.

commonCauses.title: Triggers
commonCauses.detail: Colds and other illness, strong sunlight, tiredness, stress or periods can bring on a cold sore.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about antiviral cream, which works best when started at the first tingle
Use cold sore patches to protect the sore
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Wash your hands after touching the sore
Use lip balm with sun protection
avoid: Kissing, especially babies, while you have a cold sore
Oral sex while you have a cold sore
Sharing cups, cutlery, towels or lip balm
Touching the sore and then your eyes
seeDoctorIf: A cold sore has not started to heal within 10 days
The cold sore is very large or painful
You keep getting cold sores
You are pregnant and have a cold sore

name: Constipation
summary: Constipation means pooing less often than usual or having hard, difficult-to-pass poo. It is common and usually improves with more fibre, fluids and activity.
redFlags: Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
Heavy bleeding from the bottom
urgentFlags: Constipation with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
Blood in your poo
Constipation with severe tiredness and weight loss

commonCauses.title: Not enough fibre or fluid
commonCauses.detail: A diet low in fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, or not drinking enough.

commonCauses.title: Lack of activity
commonCauses.detail: Sitting or lying down for long periods slows the bowel.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Strong painkillers, iron tablets and some other medicines commonly cause constipation.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy or changes in routine
commonCauses.detail: Hormone changes, travel or ignoring the urge to go.

commonCauses.title: Irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Constipation that alternates with diarrhoea and bloating.

selfCare: Gradually add more fibre such as fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrains
Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day
Be more active, even a daily walk can help
Go to the toilet when you feel the urge and resting your feet on a low stool can make pooing easier
Ask a pharmacist about laxatives if these changes do not help, following the pack instructions
avoid: Using laxatives every day for long periods without advice
Colon cleansing or 'detox' products, which are unproven
Ignoring the urge to poo
seeDoctorIf: You are not getting better with self-care
You are often constipated
You have a persistent change in bowel habit lasting 3 weeks or more
You have lost weight without trying, or feel tired all the time
You need to take laxatives regularly

name: Constipation in a child
summary: Constipation is common in children and can usually be helped with more fluids, fibre and a regular toilet routine. Some children need medicine from a doctor.
redFlags: A swollen tummy with green vomit
Severe tummy pain, or a baby who is floppy and not feeding
urgentFlags: Constipation in a baby in the first few weeks of life
Blood in the poo
Constipation with a high temperature, vomiting or a very swollen tummy
Weakness in the legs or problems walking

commonCauses.title: Not enough fibre or fluid
commonCauses.detail: Very common, especially in fussy eaters.

commonCauses.title: Holding in poo
commonCauses.detail: Because of pain, fear of the toilet, or during toilet training.

commonCauses.title: Changes in routine or diet
commonCauses.detail: Starting solids, switching to cow's milk or travel.

commonCauses.title: Medical causes
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, conditions affecting the bowel, nerves or thyroid.

selfCare: Give plenty of fluids, especially water
Offer fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrains if your child is eating solids
Encourage a regular toilet routine after meals, with a footstool so their knees are higher than their hips
Praise your child for using the toilet, even if nothing happens
avoid: Giving adult laxatives or suppositories without advice
Punishing or pressuring a child over toilet use
Adding extra water to formula milk
seeDoctorIf: Constipation has not improved with diet changes after 2 weeks
Your child is soiling their pants
Your child is in pain when pooing or has a sore bottom
Your child is not growing well or losing weight

name: Cough
summary: A cough is usually caused by a virus such as a cold or flu and gets better on its own within 3 to 4 weeks. A cough lasting longer than 3 weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing, gasping or unable to speak in full sentences
Lips or skin turning blue, grey or very pale
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood
Cough with chest pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back
Sudden confusion or very drowsy
urgentFlags: Cough is very bad or getting worse quickly
Feeling very unwell, or a high temperature that is not settling
Chest pain or finding it hard to breathe
Coughing up small streaks of blood
Swollen, painful glands in the side of the neck

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause; the cough can last several weeks after other symptoms.

commonCauses.title: Chest infection
commonCauses.detail: Such as bronchitis, with a chesty cough and mucus.

commonCauses.title: Asthma and allergies
commonCauses.detail: Cough often worse at night or with exercise.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux and postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Can cause a long-lasting cough.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and long-term lung conditions
commonCauses.detail: Such as COPD; a persistent cough needs checking.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Try hot lemon and honey (not for babies under 1)
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches, following the pack instructions
Stay at home if you have a high temperature or feel unwell
Cover coughs and wash your hands often
avoid: Expecting antibiotics, which do not help viral coughs
Smoking
Giving cough medicines to young children unless advised by a pharmacist
seeDoctorIf: You have had a cough for more than 3 weeks
You are losing weight for no reason
You have a weakened immune system
Your cough keeps coming back

name: Coughing up blood
summary: Coughing up blood can be caused by a chest infection or a nosebleed, but it can also be a sign of something serious. It should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Coughing up more than just a few spots or streaks of blood
Coughing up blood with difficulty breathing
Coughing up blood with a very fast heartbeat
Coughing up blood with pain in the chest or upper back
Coughing up blood with a painful, swollen leg
urgentFlags: A few small spots, flecks or streaks of blood in your phlegm
Blood in phlegm with a fever or feeling unwell

commonCauses.title: Chest infection
commonCauses.detail: A heavy cough can cause small streaks of blood.

commonCauses.title: Nosebleed or bleeding gums
commonCauses.detail: Blood from the nose or mouth can be mistaken for blood from the lungs.

commonCauses.title: Pulmonary embolism
commonCauses.detail: A blood clot in the lungs, often with breathlessness and chest pain.

commonCauses.title: Long-term lung conditions
commonCauses.detail: Bronchiectasis, tuberculosis or COPD.

commonCauses.title: Lung cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but more likely in smokers and older adults.

selfCare: Note how much blood there is and what it looks like
Arrange to be seen by a doctor even if it stops
avoid: Ignoring blood in your phlegm, even if it happens once
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: You have coughed up any blood that has not been checked
You also have a cough for more than 3 weeks or weight loss

name: Coughing up phlegm or mucus
summary: Coughing up phlegm is common with colds and chest infections, and helps clear the airways. Yellow or green phlegm alone does not mean you need antibiotics.
redFlags: Severe difficulty breathing, or lips or skin turning blue or grey
Coughing up more than a few streaks of blood
Confusion, very fast breathing or feeling extremely unwell
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell or symptoms getting worse
Blood-stained mucus
Fast breathing, chest pain or shortness of breath
Being over 65, pregnant, or having a long-term heart, lung or kidney condition with a chest infection

commonCauses.title: Chest infection (bronchitis)
commonCauses.detail: Usually viral and clears in 1 to 3 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Pneumonia
commonCauses.detail: Infection of the lungs with fever, breathlessness and feeling very unwell.

commonCauses.title: Postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Mucus from the nose running down the throat.

commonCauses.title: COPD, asthma or bronchiectasis
commonCauses.detail: Long-term lung conditions can cause daily phlegm.

commonCauses.title: Smoking
commonCauses.detail: Causes ongoing mucus production.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids to loosen the mucus
Breathe in steam from a warm shower
Raise your head with extra pillows at night
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or aches, following the pack instructions
avoid: Smoking
Assuming coloured phlegm needs antibiotics
Cough suppressants for a chesty cough unless advised by a pharmacist
seeDoctorIf: Your cough has lasted more than 3 weeks
You keep getting chest infections
You cough up phlegm most days

name: Cuts and grazes
summary: Most small cuts and grazes can be treated at home and heal within a few days. Deep cuts, heavy bleeding or signs of infection need medical attention.
redFlags: Bleeding that is heavy, spurting, or will not stop after 10 minutes of firm pressure
A deep wound to the chest, tummy, neck or head
An object stuck in the wound
Numbness, tingling or being unable to move the area beyond the cut
urgentFlags: A cut that is gaping, longer than about 5cm or that may need stitches
A cut from a human or animal bite
Dirt or debris that you cannot clean out
Signs of infection: increasing pain, swelling, redness, pus or a high temperature

commonCauses.title: Everyday accidents
commonCauses.detail: Knives, glass, falls and sports injuries.

commonCauses.title: Bites
commonCauses.detail: Human and animal bites carry a high risk of infection.

selfCare: Stop the bleeding by pressing firmly with a clean cloth and raising the area
Clean the wound under running tap water
Pat dry and cover with a plaster or sterile dressing
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
avoid: Using antiseptic on the wound, which can damage tissue; clean water is enough
Removing an object stuck deep in a wound
Picking at scabs
seeDoctorIf: A wound has not healed after 2 weeks
You are unsure if your tetanus vaccination is up to date and the wound is dirty
You have diabetes and a cut on your foot

name: Dark, cloudy or smelly urine
summary: Dark pee usually means you need to drink more. Cloudy or strong-smelling pee can also be a sign of a urine infection.
redFlags: Dark pee with confusion, fainting or extreme drowsiness
Not having peed all day
urgentFlags: Dark pee with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, or pale poo
Cloudy pee with burning, a high temperature or pain in your back or side
Brown or cola-coloured pee after intense exercise or a crush injury, with muscle pain
Dark pee that stays dark even after drinking more

commonCauses.title: Not drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Concentrated pee is darker and smells stronger.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Cloudy, strong-smelling pee with burning and needing to pee often.

commonCauses.title: Food and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Asparagus, beetroot, vitamins and some medicines change pee colour or smell.

commonCauses.title: Liver problems
commonCauses.detail: Dark brown pee with yellow skin or eyes can be a sign of a liver or gallbladder problem.

selfCare: Drink enough fluids so your pee is pale yellow
Drink more in hot weather and when exercising
Check whether a new food, vitamin or medicine could explain the change
avoid: Ignoring dark pee that comes with yellow skin or eyes
Using cranberry products instead of getting a suspected infection checked
seeDoctorIf: Your pee stays dark or cloudy for more than a few days despite drinking more
Your pee is frothy or foamy most of the time
You keep getting urine infections

name: Dehydration
summary: Dehydration means your body loses more fluid than it takes in. It is common with vomiting, diarrhoea, heat or exercise and can usually be treated by drinking more.
redFlags: Confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Not peeing all day
A fast heartbeat or fast breathing with feeling very unwell
Sunken eyes, cold hands and feet, or blotchy skin in a child
A seizure (fit)
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down
Feeling dizzy or lightheaded when standing that does not go away
Dark pee or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Dehydration in a baby, young child, older person or someone with diabetes or kidney disease

commonCauses.title: Diarrhoea and vomiting
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause, especially in children and older people.

commonCauses.title: Heat and exercise
commonCauses.detail: Sweating a lot in hot weather or during exercise.

commonCauses.title: Fever
commonCauses.detail: A high temperature increases fluid loss.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Alcohol and diuretics make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: High blood sugar
commonCauses.detail: Uncontrolled diabetes causes thirst and peeing a lot.

selfCare: Drink fluids often in small sips, aiming for pale yellow pee
Use oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy if you have diarrhoea or vomiting
Rest somewhere cool
Keep giving breast or formula milk to babies, little and often
avoid: Alcohol and lots of caffeine while dehydrated
Sugary fizzy drinks or undiluted fruit juice if you have diarrhoea
Giving young children sports drinks instead of oral rehydration solution
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not improved after drinking more fluids
You often feel very thirsty
You are peeing a lot or losing weight

name: Diarrhoea
summary: Diarrhoea is loose, watery poo, usually caused by a stomach bug. In adults it normally gets better within 5 to 7 days.
redFlags: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Bleeding from the bottom that is heavy or will not stop
Severe stomach pain or a hard, swollen stomach
Confusion, fainting or extreme drowsiness
Signs of sepsis such as cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
urgentFlags: Bloody or black poo
Signs of dehydration such as dizziness, very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Being unable to keep fluids down
Diarrhoea after recent travel abroad or a recent hospital stay or course of antibiotics
Diarrhoea with a weakened immune system, kidney disease or diabetes

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug (gastroenteritis)
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause; often with vomiting, cramps and a mild temperature.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Starts within hours to days of eating contaminated food.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Antibiotics and several other medicines can cause loose poo.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance or irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Diarrhoea that comes and goes may be linked to certain foods or IBS.

commonCauses.title: Inflammatory bowel disease
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, ongoing diarrhoea with blood or mucus can be due to Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.

selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids such as water in small sips; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy helps replace lost salts
Eat when you feel able; plain foods are usually easiest
Wash your hands with soap and water after the toilet and before preparing food
Stay off work or school until 48 hours after the last episode
A pharmacist can advise if anti-diarrhoea medicine is suitable for you
avoid: Fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse
Anti-diarrhoea medicine if you have a high temperature or blood in your poo, unless a doctor advises it
Swimming pools for 2 weeks after the diarrhoea stops
seeDoctorIf: Diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days
Diarrhoea keeps coming back
You have lost weight without trying
Your bowel habits have changed for 3 weeks or more

name: Diarrhoea in babies and children
summary: Diarrhoea in children is usually caused by a stomach bug and gets better within 5 to 7 days. Keeping them drinking is the most important thing.
redFlags: Blood in the poo with your child seeming very unwell
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
Signs of severe dehydration such as no wet nappies or not peeing all day, cold hands and feet, or sunken eyes
Severe tummy pain or a swollen tummy
Green vomit with diarrhoea
urgentFlags: Signs of dehydration such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth, no tears or a sunken soft spot on the head
Blood in the poo
A baby under 6 months with diarrhoea and a high temperature
Diarrhoea with vomiting for more than 2 days in a child under 5

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug
commonCauses.detail: Viruses such as rotavirus and norovirus are the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: From contaminated food or water.

commonCauses.title: Antibiotics
commonCauses.detail: Can upset the normal balance of gut bacteria.

commonCauses.title: Toddler's diarrhoea
commonCauses.detail: Loose poo with undigested food in a well, growing toddler; often linked to lots of juice.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance or allergy
commonCauses.detail: For example cow's milk protein allergy in babies.

selfCare: Keep breast or formula feeding; offer extra fluids little and often
Use oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy if your child is at risk of dehydration
Offer food when your child feels able
Wash hands thoroughly and keep children off nursery or school until 48 hours after the last episode
avoid: Fruit juice or fizzy drinks
Anti-diarrhoea medicines for children under 12
Swimming pools for 2 weeks after the diarrhoea stops
seeDoctorIf: Diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days
Diarrhoea keeps coming back
Your child is not gaining weight or is losing weight

name: Difficulty peeing or weak flow
summary: A weak flow, straining or dribbling is common in older men and often due to an enlarged prostate. Suddenly being unable to pee at all is an emergency.
redFlags: Being suddenly unable to pee at all, often with a painful, swollen lower tummy
Difficulty peeing with new numbness around the genitals or bottom, or weakness in the legs and back pain
urgentFlags: Difficulty peeing with a high temperature or pain in your back or side
