Blood in your pee
Difficulty peeing after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Very common in men over 50, causing a weak flow, straining and getting up at night.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: A bladder or prostate infection can make peeing difficult and painful.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some cold remedies, antihistamines and other medicines can make it harder to pee.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: A full bowel can press on the bladder.

commonCauses.title: Narrowing of the urethra or prostate cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes that need tests.

selfCare: Cut down on alcohol, caffeine and fizzy drinks, especially in the evening
Take your time when peeing and try peeing again a few minutes later (double voiding)
Treat constipation if you have it
avoid: Over-the-counter decongestants and some antihistamines, which can make it harder to pee
Assuming it is just age and not getting checked
seeDoctorIf: You have a weak flow, straining or dribbling
You feel your bladder does not empty fully
You get up several times at night to pee
You are worried about your prostate

name: Difficulty swallowing
summary: Difficulty swallowing means food or drink is hard to get down or feels stuck. A short-lived problem with a sore throat is common, but ongoing swallowing difficulty should always be checked.
redFlags: Unable to swallow saliva, or drooling
Difficulty breathing, or noisy high-pitched breathing
Food stuck in the throat or chest that will not move and you cannot swallow anything
Sudden difficulty swallowing with face drooping, weakness or slurred speech
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
urgentFlags: Ongoing difficulty swallowing
Coughing or choking while eating or drinking
Feeling that food sticks in your throat or chest
Bringing food back up, or a wet, gurgly voice after eating
Losing weight without trying

commonCauses.title: Sore throat or tonsillitis
commonCauses.detail: Pain and swelling make swallowing uncomfortable for a few days.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Can inflame or narrow the food pipe.

commonCauses.title: Neurological conditions
commonCauses.detail: Stroke, Parkinson's disease and other conditions can affect the swallowing muscles.

commonCauses.title: Narrowing or growth in the food pipe
commonCauses.detail: Including, less commonly, cancer of the oesophagus.

selfCare: Sit upright to eat and drink, and stay upright for a while afterwards
Take small bites and chew well
Choose softer, moist foods while you are waiting to be seen
avoid: Eating while lying down or rushing meals
Ignoring swallowing problems that keep happening
seeDoctorIf: You keep having difficulty swallowing
You get frequent chest infections
You have heartburn or acid reflux most days

name: Discharge from the ear
summary: Fluid leaking from the ear is often caused by an ear infection or a perforated (burst) eardrum. It should be checked by a doctor or pharmacist.
redFlags: Clear fluid or blood from the ear after a head injury
Ear discharge with a stiff neck, severe headache, confusion or a rash that does not fade
Ear discharge with face drooping or sudden severe dizziness
urgentFlags: Ear discharge with a high temperature or feeling generally unwell
Swelling, redness or pain behind the ear
Ear discharge with hearing loss
Discharge after a loud bang or an injury to the ear

commonCauses.title: Middle ear infection with a perforated eardrum
commonCauses.detail: Pain often eases once pus drains; the eardrum usually heals within weeks.

commonCauses.title: Outer ear infection
commonCauses.detail: Itching, pain and discharge from the ear canal.

commonCauses.title: Earwax
commonCauses.detail: Soft wax can look like discharge.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Damage to the ear canal or eardrum from cotton buds or loud noise.

selfCare: Wipe away discharge from the outer ear with clean cotton wool
Keep the ear dry: avoid swimming and cover the ear in the shower
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Poking cotton buds or anything else into the ear
Using ear drops not recommended by a doctor or pharmacist if the eardrum may be burst
Swimming until the ear has healed
seeDoctorIf: You have any ear discharge that has not been checked
Discharge keeps coming back
Hearing has not returned to normal after the infection clears

name: Discharge from the penis
summary: Discharge from the penis that is not urine or semen is often caused by a sexually transmitted infection. A sexual health clinic or doctor can test and treat it.
redFlags: Being unable to pee at all
Severe pain, swelling and redness of the genitals or groin with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Discharge with testicle pain or swelling
Discharge with a high temperature
Discharge with joint pain or a rash

commonCauses.title: Chlamydia or gonorrhoea
commonCauses.detail: Common sexually transmitted infections that often cause discharge and burning when peeing.

commonCauses.title: Non-gonococcal urethritis
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation of the tube that carries urine, often caused by an infection.

commonCauses.title: Balanitis or thrush
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation under the foreskin with a thick discharge, redness and soreness.

commonCauses.title: Trichomoniasis
commonCauses.detail: A sexually transmitted infection that can cause thin white discharge.

selfCare: Get tested at a sexual health clinic or by a doctor
Avoid sex until you and your partner have been tested and treated
Wash under the foreskin gently with water each day
avoid: Taking leftover or online antibiotics without a diagnosis
Having sex, including oral sex, until treatment is finished
seeDoctorIf: You have any unusual discharge from your penis
A partner has been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection
Symptoms come back after treatment

name: Dizziness or light-headedness
summary: Feeling dizzy, light-headed or off-balance is common and usually not serious. It often passes on its own and can be caused by things like standing up quickly, dehydration or an ear problem.
redFlags: Dizziness with chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or shortness of breath
Dizziness with weakness or numbness in the face, arm or leg, or a drooping face
Dizziness with slurred speech, sudden confusion or loss of vision
Dizziness with a sudden, severe headache
Fainting or collapsing and not recovering quickly
urgentFlags: Dizziness with a very high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
Dizziness with repeated vomiting so you cannot keep fluids down
Dizziness after a head injury
Dizziness with new double or blurred vision that has now passed

commonCauses.title: Standing up quickly
commonCauses.detail: A brief drop in blood pressure when you stand can make you light-headed for a few seconds.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration, heat or missed meals
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking or eating enough, or being too hot, can make you feel faint.

commonCauses.title: Inner ear problems
commonCauses.detail: Ear infections, labyrinthitis and other inner ear conditions can cause dizziness or spinning.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety or stress
commonCauses.detail: Anxiety and fast breathing can cause light-headedness.

commonCauses.title: Medicines or low blood sugar
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, and low blood sugar in people with diabetes, can cause dizziness.

selfCare: Sit or lie down until the dizziness passes
Stand up slowly, especially from lying down
Drink plenty of fluids and eat regular meals
Move carefully and turn on lights at night to avoid falls
Get plenty of rest and sleep
avoid: Driving, climbing ladders or using machinery while dizzy
Alcohol, caffeine and smoking, which can make dizziness worse
Bending down suddenly
seeDoctorIf: Dizziness will not go away or keeps coming back
You also have hearing loss or ringing in the ears
You have fainted or nearly fainted
You think a medicine may be causing it

name: Double vision
summary: Double vision is when you see two images of a single object. It can come from a problem in one eye or from the eyes not lining up, and it should always be checked.
redFlags: Double or blurred vision with a severe headache or an enlarged pupil
Double vision after a head injury
Double vision with face drooping, weakness, numbness, slurred speech or loss of balance
A drooping eyelid that started suddenly with double vision
urgentFlags: Double vision that has started suddenly
Double vision with eye pain

commonCauses.title: Eye surface or lens problems
commonCauses.detail: Dry eyes, astigmatism or cataracts can cause a ghost image in one eye.

commonCauses.title: Squint or eye muscle problems
commonCauses.detail: When the eyes do not line up, each sees a slightly different image.

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes, high blood pressure or other conditions can affect the nerves that move the eyes.

commonCauses.title: Stroke, head injury or thyroid eye disease
commonCauses.detail: More serious causes that need prompt assessment.

Do not drive until your vision has been checked
Take care on stairs and steps
avoid: Driving or operating machinery
Waiting to see if sudden double vision goes away
seeDoctorIf: You think you or your child might have double vision, even if it comes and goes

name: Dry mouth
summary: A dry mouth is rarely serious and is often caused by dehydration, medicines, mouth breathing or anxiety. Simple measures usually help.

urgentFlags: Dry mouth with constant thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss
Dry mouth with signs of dehydration that are not improving with drinking

commonCauses.title: Dehydration
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking enough, sweating or being ill.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines list dry mouth as a side effect.

commonCauses.title: Mouth breathing

commonCauses.title: Health conditions

Ask a pharmacist about saliva substitutes, sprays or gels
Use a humidifier at night

avoid: Alcohol, including alcohol-based mouthwash

seeDoctorIf: Your mouth is still dry after a few weeks of home or pharmacy treatment

name: Dry, cracked or eczema-prone skin

urgentFlags: Eczema that is suddenly much worse, weeping, crusted or painful
Red, hot, swollen skin that is spreading

commonCauses.detail: Cold weather, central heating and frequent hand washing dry the skin.

commonCauses.title: Atopic eczema

commonCauses.title: Contact dermatitis

commonCauses.title: Underactive thyroid or ageing
commonCauses.detail: Can make skin drier.

You think your skin might be infected

Something stuck in the ear
A child under 2 with earache in both ears

commonCauses.title: Middle ear infection
commonCauses.detail: Often follows a cold; common in children and usually clears in 3 to 5 days.

commonCauses.title: Outer ear infection (otitis externa)
commonCauses.detail: Pain, itching and discharge, often after swimming.

commonCauses.title: Earwax or a blocked ear
commonCauses.detail: Can cause discomfort and muffled hearing.

commonCauses.title: Pain from nearby areas
commonCauses.detail: Sore throat, tonsillitis, toothache, teething or jaw joint problems can be felt in the ear.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Hold a warm or cold flannel against the ear
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Ask a pharmacist for advice; in some countries they can treat ear infections
avoid: Putting cotton buds, fingers or anything else in the ear
Getting the ear wet if it is infected or discharging
Using olive oil or drops if the eardrum might be burst
seeDoctorIf: You or your child keep getting earache
Earache does not improve after 3 days
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system and an ear infection

name: Elbow and arm pain
summary: Elbow and arm pain is usually caused by overuse, such as tennis elbow, and gets better with rest and time.
redFlags: Arm pain with chest pain, breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick
An arm or elbow that looks deformed after an injury
Sudden weakness or numbness of the arm with face drooping or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Being unable to move the elbow or arm after an injury
A red, hot, swollen elbow, especially with a high temperature
Pain with tingling or numbness that is not going away

commonCauses.title: Tennis or golfer's elbow
commonCauses.detail: Pain on the outside or inside of the elbow from overuse of forearm muscles.

commonCauses.title: Bursitis
commonCauses.detail: A soft swelling at the back of the elbow.

commonCauses.title: Trapped nerve
commonCauses.detail: Tingling in the arm or fingers from a nerve in the neck or elbow.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Sprains, dislocations or broken bones after a fall.

selfCare: Rest the arm and avoid the activity that causes pain
Use a cold pack wrapped in a towel
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, or use an anti-inflammatory gel, following the pack instructions
Gently stretch and strengthen the forearm as pain eases
avoid: Repetitive gripping or lifting with the painful arm
Keeping the arm completely still for a long time
seeDoctorIf: Pain has not improved after 2 weeks
You have tingling, numbness or weakness in your hand
Pain is affecting work or sleep

name: Erection problems
summary: Difficulty getting or keeping an erection is very common and can be linked to stress, tiredness, alcohol, or health conditions such as heart disease and diabetes. It is worth seeing a doctor, as treatments work well.
redFlags: An erection lasting more than 4 hours, or a painful erection not caused by sexual arousal
Erection problems with chest pain, breathlessness or pain spreading to the arm or jaw
urgentFlags: Sudden erection problems with new numbness around the genitals, bottom or legs
A painful bend in the penis that appeared suddenly or after an injury

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or relationship issues
commonCauses.detail: Often the cause when erections still happen at other times, such as in the morning.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, smoking and tiredness
commonCauses.detail: These commonly affect erections.

commonCauses.title: Blood vessel and heart conditions
commonCauses.detail: High blood pressure, high cholesterol and heart disease reduce blood flow to the penis.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes and hormone problems
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes can affect nerves and blood vessels; low testosterone is less common.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some blood pressure medicines and antidepressants can cause erection problems.

selfCare: Cut down on alcohol and stop smoking
Be more active and aim for a healthy weight
Find ways to manage stress and talk openly with your partner
Do not stop a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor
avoid: Erection pills bought online from unregulated sellers, which may be fake or unsafe
Recreational drugs, which can make erection problems worse
seeDoctorIf: Erection problems keep happening for more than a few weeks
You also have symptoms such as feeling thirsty, peeing a lot or tiredness
You think a medicine might be causing it
It is affecting your wellbeing or relationship

name: Excessive daytime sleepiness
summary: Feeling very sleepy during the day is often caused by not getting enough good-quality sleep. When it happens despite enough sleep, it can be a sign of a sleep disorder or other health problem.
redFlags: Sudden drowsiness, confusion or difficulty waking someone
Drowsiness after a head injury
Drowsiness after taking too much medicine, alcohol or drugs
urgentFlags: Falling asleep or nearly falling asleep while driving
Sudden loss of muscle strength when laughing or with strong emotion
Sleepiness with breathlessness, morning headaches or swollen ankles

commonCauses.title: Not enough sleep
commonCauses.detail: Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours.

commonCauses.title: Sleep apnoea
commonCauses.detail: Interrupted breathing at night causes poor-quality sleep.

commonCauses.title: Medicines and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines cause drowsiness.

commonCauses.title: Depression, anaemia or an underactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Can make you feel tired and sleepy.

commonCauses.title: Narcolepsy
commonCauses.detail: A rare condition causing sudden sleep attacks.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and aim for enough sleep
Get daylight and physical activity during the day
Limit alcohol and caffeine, especially in the evening
Take a short break and do not drive if you feel sleepy
avoid: Driving or using machinery when sleepy
Relying on caffeine or energy drinks to stay awake
seeDoctorIf: You feel very sleepy even after enough sleep
You snore loudly or someone has seen you stop breathing in your sleep
Sleepiness is affecting work, study or safety
You think a medicine is making you sleepy

name: Excessive sweating
summary: Sweating more than usual is often harmless and may run in families. New sweating, sweating at night or sweating with other symptoms can have an underlying cause.
redFlags: Sweating with chest pain, pain spreading to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or breathlessness
Sweating with confusion, shakiness and drowsiness, especially if you have diabetes
urgentFlags: Sweating with a high temperature and feeling unwell
Sweating with a racing heartbeat, tremor and weight loss

commonCauses.title: Primary hyperhidrosis
commonCauses.detail: Excessive sweating of the hands, feet, armpits or face with no other cause; often starts young.

commonCauses.title: Menopause
commonCauses.detail: Hot flushes and night sweats.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Stress and worry increase sweating.

commonCauses.title: Medicines or medical conditions
commonCauses.detail: Some antidepressants, an overactive thyroid, infections, low blood sugar or, rarely, cancer.

selfCare: Use a strong antiperspirant, applied at night to dry skin
Wear loose, breathable clothing and moisture-wicking socks
Change socks often and avoid tight footwear
Cut down on alcohol, caffeine and spicy food if they are triggers
avoid: Clothes made from synthetic fibres that trap sweat
Unregulated tablets or devices sold online
seeDoctorIf: Sweating is affecting your daily life
You sweat at night for no obvious reason
You started sweating more suddenly
You also have weight loss or a high temperature

name: Eye injury or something in the eye
summary: Small specks of dust or grit can often be rinsed out with clean water. Chemicals in the eye, sharp or high-speed objects, and injuries that affect vision need emergency care.
redFlags: A strong chemical such as bleach or oven cleaner has got into the eye (keep rinsing with water while getting help)
A sharp object has pierced the eye, or something hit it at high speed
Any change in sight after an eye injury
Severe eye pain, or blood or pus coming from the eye
Cannot move the eye or keep it open
Headache, light sensitivity or being sick after an eye injury
urgentFlags: The injured eye is not getting better after 24 hours
The eye is very painful
A child has injured their eye
It still feels like something is in the eye after rinsing

commonCauses.title: Dust, grit or an eyelash
commonCauses.detail: Usually washes out with tears or clean water.

commonCauses.title: Scratch on the eye surface (corneal abrasion)
commonCauses.detail: Painful and watery, often healing within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Blunt injury
commonCauses.detail: A blow can cause a black eye or bleeding inside the eye.

commonCauses.title: Chemical splash
commonCauses.detail: Household or workplace chemicals can cause serious damage.

selfCare: Wash the eye with plenty of clean, lukewarm water
Follow the advice on the packaging if a household product gets in the eye
Hold a cold compress gently on a black eye
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Wear eye protection for DIY, gardening and power tools
avoid: Trying to remove anything stuck in the eye
Rubbing or pressing on the eye
Wearing contact lenses until the eye has healed
seeDoctorIf: Your eye remains irritated or watery after a few days
A black eye is not fading after 2 weeks

name: Eye pain
summary: Eye pain is often caused by minor problems such as dry eyes, a stye or conjunctivitis. Severe pain, or pain with redness and changes to your vision, needs urgent assessment.
redFlags: Eye pain that started suddenly and is severe
Eye pain with loss of vision
Red eye with a severe headache and feeling sick
Eye pain and vision loss while wearing contact lenses
Severe pain or loss of vision after eye surgery in the last 4 weeks
An injury to the eye, or something stuck in it
urgentFlags: Severe eye pain
Sensitivity to light
Changes to your vision, such as blurring or colours looking different
A very red eye with pain
Eye pain that keeps you awake at night

commonCauses.title: Dry or tired eyes
commonCauses.detail: Can cause aching, burning or gritty pain.

commonCauses.title: Conjunctivitis or blepharitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection or inflammation cause soreness, redness and grittiness.

commonCauses.title: Stye or chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A painful lump on the eyelid.

commonCauses.title: Something in the eye or a scratch
commonCauses.detail: A speck of dust or a scratch on the surface can be very painful.

commonCauses.title: Serious eye conditions
commonCauses.detail: Acute glaucoma, iritis, corneal infection and optic nerve inflammation can cause pain and need urgent care.

selfCare: Rinse the eye with clean water if you think something is in it
Use a cool compress for soreness, or a warm compress for a stye
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Remove contact lenses and leave them out until the eye is better
avoid: Rubbing the eye
Trying to remove anything stuck in the coloured part of the eye
Wearing contact lenses while your eye is painful
seeDoctorIf: Mild eye pain does not improve within a few days
Eye pain keeps coming back
You also have headaches or blurred vision that come and go

name: Eye strain or tired eyes
summary: Eye strain is tired, aching or burning eyes after long periods of close work, reading, driving or using screens. It is uncomfortable but does not damage the eyes, and usually settles with rest.
redFlags: Sudden loss or change of vision
Severe eye pain with a red eye, headache and feeling sick
urgentFlags: Eye pain with redness or sensitivity to light
New double vision

commonCauses.title: Screen use
commonCauses.detail: Focusing on screens reduces blinking and tires the eye muscles.

commonCauses.title: Uncorrected vision
commonCauses.detail: Needing glasses, or an out-of-date prescription, makes the eyes work harder.

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes and lighting
commonCauses.detail: Glare, poor lighting and dry air add to strain.

selfCare: Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds
Set screens about an arm's length away and slightly below eye level
Reduce glare and use good lighting
Use lubricating eye drops if your eyes feel dry
Have a sight test to check whether you need glasses
avoid: Using screens for hours without breaks
Reading in dim light
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms continue despite screen breaks
You have frequent headaches with eye strain
Your vision seems to be changing

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology – Eye strain

name: Eyelid twitching
summary: A twitching eyelid is very common and almost always harmless. It is often linked to tiredness, stress, caffeine or eye strain and usually goes away on its own.
redFlags: Twitching with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
A drooping eyelid that comes on suddenly with a severe headache or double vision
urgentFlags: The eyelid closes completely with each twitch and you cannot open it
Twitching with a red, painful eye or discharge

commonCauses.title: Tiredness and stress
commonCauses.detail: The most common triggers for a harmless eyelid twitch.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Too much coffee, tea, energy drinks or alcohol can trigger twitching.

commonCauses.title: Eye strain and dry eyes
commonCauses.detail: Long screen use and dry or irritated eyes can cause twitching.

commonCauses.title: Blepharospasm or hemifacial spasm
commonCauses.detail: Rare conditions causing persistent forced closing of the eyelids or twitching of one side of the face.

selfCare: Get more sleep and try to reduce stress
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Take regular breaks from screens
Use lubricating eye drops if your eyes feel dry
avoid: Rubbing or pressing on the eye
Supplements marketed as cures for eye twitching
seeDoctorIf: Twitching lasts more than a few weeks
Twitching spreads to other parts of your face
Your eyelid droops
The eye becomes red, swollen or has discharge

name: Face drooping or facial weakness
summary: Sudden drooping or weakness of one side of the face can be a sign of a stroke and is an emergency. A common other cause is Bell's palsy, which also needs to be seen quickly.
redFlags: Face drooping on one side that came on suddenly
Cannot lift both arms and keep them there
Slurred or garbled speech, or trouble understanding
Sudden confusion, loss of vision, loss of balance or severe headache
urgentFlags: Weakness of one side of the face that developed over a day or two, with no other symptoms
Cannot close one eye fully
Facial weakness with pain behind the ear or a rash on the ear

commonCauses.title: Stroke
commonCauses.detail: Loss of blood supply to part of the brain; face drooping is one of the main warning signs.

commonCauses.title: Bell's palsy
commonCauses.detail: Temporary weakness of one side of the face, usually developing over a few days; treatment works best if started within 72 hours.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or shingles
commonCauses.detail: Infections around the ear can affect the facial nerve.

selfCare: Use the FAST check: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services
If a doctor has diagnosed Bell's palsy, protect the eye with eye drops or ointment as advised
Tape the affected eye closed at night if a doctor advises it
Eat soft food and chew on the unaffected side
avoid: Waiting to see if facial drooping improves on its own
Driving yourself to hospital
Rubbing an eye that cannot close properly
seeDoctorIf: Bell's palsy has not started to improve after 3 weeks
You have ongoing eye irritation from not closing the eye
Facial weakness is affecting your mood, eating or drinking

name: Fainting or passing out
summary: Fainting is when you lose consciousness for a short time, usually because blood flow to the brain drops briefly. It is often not serious, but it should be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Not breathing, or cannot be woken within 1 minute
Not fully recovered, or has difficulty speaking or moving
Chest pain or a pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat
Fainted during exercise or while lying down
Shaking or jerking (a possible seizure)
Seriously hurt themselves when they fell
urgentFlags: Fainting more than once in a short time
Fainting with shortness of breath
Fainting during pregnancy
Fainting in someone with a known heart condition

commonCauses.title: Vasovagal faint
commonCauses.detail: A common, usually harmless faint triggered by standing for long periods, heat, pain, fear or the sight of blood.

commonCauses.title: Low blood pressure on standing
commonCauses.detail: Standing up quickly, dehydration or some medicines can make blood pressure drop.

commonCauses.title: Not eating or drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Low fluids or low blood sugar can lead to fainting.

commonCauses.title: Heart rhythm or heart problems
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, fainting is caused by a heart problem, which needs medical assessment.

selfCare: If you feel faint, lie down and raise your legs, or sit with your head between your knees
Drink fluids and eat something once you feel better
Get up slowly after fainting and rest
Drink enough fluids and avoid standing still for long periods if you are prone to fainting
If someone faints, lay them on their back and raise their legs, and check they are breathing
avoid: Driving until a doctor has checked why you fainted
Getting up quickly straight after fainting
Giving food or drink to someone who is not fully awake
seeDoctorIf: You have fainted, even once, to find out the cause
You often feel faint or light-headed
You think a medicine may be making you faint

name: Farting and burping a lot
summary: Passing wind and burping are normal, but some foods and habits can make them happen more often. Changes to diet and eating habits usually help.
redFlags: Not passing any poo or wind at all, with a swollen stomach and vomiting
Severe stomach pain
urgentFlags: Wind with blood in your poo
Wind with a high temperature and diarrhoea that is getting worse

commonCauses.title: Diet
commonCauses.detail: Beans, lentils, cabbage, onions, dried fruit and fizzy drinks produce more gas.

commonCauses.title: Swallowing air
commonCauses.detail: Eating quickly, chewing gum and smoking can make you swallow air.

commonCauses.title: Constipation or irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Both commonly cause trapped wind and bloating.

commonCauses.title: Food intolerance
commonCauses.detail: For example lactose intolerance or coeliac disease.

selfCare: Eat smaller meals slowly and chew with your mouth closed
Cut down on foods that give you wind
Exercise regularly to help your digestion
Ask a pharmacist about remedies such as charcoal tablets or simeticone
avoid: Fizzy drinks, chewing gum and sucking sweets
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: Changes to your diet have not helped
You also have ongoing stomach pain, bloating or diarrhoea
You have lost weight without trying or noticed blood in your poo

name: Fast or noisy breathing in a baby
summary: Bronchiolitis is a common chest infection in babies under 2 that starts like a cold and can cause a cough, fast breathing and difficulty feeding. Most babies get better at home within 2 to 3 weeks.
redFlags: Your baby is struggling to breathe, grunting, or the skin is sucking in under the ribs
Pauses in breathing, or blue or grey lips or tongue
Your baby is floppy, unresponsive or very hard to wake
Your baby is too breathless to feed or make sounds
urgentFlags: Feeding less than half the usual amount over the last 2 or 3 feeds
No wet nappy for 12 hours or more
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher under 3 months, or 39C (102.2F) or higher at 3 to 6 months
Breathing faster than usual or getting worse
A baby born prematurely or with a heart or lung condition who has these symptoms

commonCauses.title: Bronchiolitis
commonCauses.detail: A viral chest infection, most often caused by RSV, common in winter.

commonCauses.title: Colds
commonCauses.detail: A blocked nose can make breathing sound noisy and make feeding harder.

commonCauses.title: Viral wheeze or asthma
commonCauses.detail: Older babies and toddlers can wheeze with colds.

selfCare: Offer smaller feeds more often
Saline nose drops from a pharmacy can help with a blocked nose before feeds
Keep your baby upright when they are awake to help breathing
Use paracetamol or ibuprofen only if your baby is old enough and distressed, following the pack instructions
Keep your baby away from smoke
avoid: Smoking near your baby, in the home or car
Cough medicines or decongestants for babies
Raising the cot mattress or putting your baby to sleep on their front
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms are not improving after 3 days
The cough has lasted more than 3 weeks
You are worried about your baby

name: Fear of social situations
summary: Social anxiety is an ongoing, overwhelming fear of social situations, such as meeting people or speaking in front of others. It is common, and talking therapies work well.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
urgentFlags: You are unable to leave the house or attend work or school
Using alcohol or drugs to cope with social situations and feeling out of control

commonCauses.title: Social anxiety disorder
commonCauses.detail: Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed that lasts a long time.

commonCauses.title: Past experiences
commonCauses.detail: Bullying, criticism or embarrassing events can contribute.

commonCauses.title: Shyness and temperament
commonCauses.detail: Some people are naturally more anxious in social situations.

commonCauses.title: Low mood or depression
commonCauses.detail: Can make social situations feel harder.

selfCare: Gradually face situations you fear in small steps
Prepare and practise for social situations
Focus on the conversation rather than on how you appear
Try CBT-based self-help resources
Use slow breathing to manage physical symptoms
avoid: Avoiding all social situations, which can make fear stronger
Using alcohol to cope
seeDoctorIf: Fear of social situations is affecting your life
You avoid work, study or seeing friends
Self-help has not helped

name: Feeling of a lump in the throat
summary: Many people feel like there is a lump or tightness in the throat even when nothing is there. It is often linked to stress, acid reflux or mucus, and is usually harmless, but real difficulty swallowing should be checked.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or noisy breathing
Unable to swallow saliva
Sudden throat tightness with swelling of the lips, tongue or face, or a rash
urgentFlags: Food actually sticking or difficulty swallowing food or drink
Pain when swallowing
Losing weight without trying
A lump you can see or feel in the neck

commonCauses.title: Globus sensation
commonCauses.detail: A harmless feeling of a lump, often worse with stress and easier when eating.

commonCauses.title: Acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Acid can irritate the throat and cause a tight feeling.

commonCauses.title: Catarrh or postnasal drip
commonCauses.detail: Mucus at the back of the throat makes you want to keep swallowing.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Tension in the throat muscles is common during anxiety.

selfCare: Sip water and swallow gently rather than repeatedly clearing your throat
Try relaxation or breathing exercises if stress makes it worse
Avoid eating late at night if you have reflux
avoid: Repeatedly clearing your throat or swallowing dry
Smoking
seeDoctorIf: The feeling lasts more than a few weeks
It is getting worse or is only on one side
You also have a hoarse voice or ear pain

name: Feeling sick (nausea)
summary: Feeling sick is common and usually caused by a stomach bug, motion sickness, pregnancy or medicines. It usually passes within a few days.
redFlags: Chest pain, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with nausea
A sudden, very severe headache with nausea
A stiff neck, sensitivity to light or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
Severe stomach pain
Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Confusion or extreme drowsiness
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down for more than a day
Signs of dehydration such as passing little or no urine, or dark urine
Nausea in pregnancy that stops you keeping food or drink down
Nausea after a head injury

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug or food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Often comes with vomiting or diarrhoea and settles within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Morning sickness is common in the first 3 months but can happen at any time of day.

commonCauses.title: Motion sickness
commonCauses.detail: Travelling by car, boat or plane.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol or migraine
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines, a hangover or a migraine can make you feel sick.

commonCauses.title: Indigestion or reflux
commonCauses.detail: Discomfort in the upper stomach with feeling sick, especially after eating.

selfCare: Get plenty of fresh air and rest
Sip small amounts of cold water or other fluids often
Eat small, plain meals such as crackers or toast when you feel able
Ginger may help some people with mild nausea
Ask a pharmacist about medicines for motion sickness if travel is the trigger
avoid: Large, greasy or strongly flavoured meals
Lying down straight after eating
Alcohol
seeDoctorIf: You keep feeling sick for more than a few days
You have also lost weight without trying
You think a medicine is causing it
You keep feeling sick and might be pregnant

name: Feeling very thirsty
summary: Feeling thirsty is normal after exercise, heat or salty food. Being thirsty all the time, especially with peeing a lot, tiredness or weight loss, can be a sign of diabetes.
redFlags: Thirst and peeing a lot with vomiting, stomach pain, deep or fast breathing, breath that smells fruity, or confusion
Extreme thirst with confusion or extreme drowsiness
urgentFlags: Thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss in a child
Thirst with feeling very unwell, dizziness or blurred vision
Thirst with a very high blood sugar reading if you have diabetes

commonCauses.title: Not drinking enough
commonCauses.detail: Especially in hot weather or with exercise.

commonCauses.title: Diet
commonCauses.detail: Salty or spicy food and alcohol.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes
commonCauses.detail: High blood sugar causes thirst, peeing a lot, tiredness and weight loss.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines cause a dry mouth or make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, kidney problems or high calcium levels.

selfCare: Drink water regularly through the day
Cut down on salty food, alcohol and sugary drinks
Notice whether you are also peeing more, tired or losing weight
avoid: Quenching thirst with sugary drinks
Ignoring persistent thirst with weight loss
seeDoctorIf: You are always thirsty and peeing a lot
You also feel tired, have blurred vision or have lost weight
You get infections such as thrush or cuts that heal slowly

name: Fever in a baby under 6 months
summary: A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher needs to be seen by a doctor straight away, even if they seem otherwise well. Young babies can become seriously ill quickly.
redFlags: A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue (on darker skin, check the palms, soles and inside the lips)
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry that is not like their normal cry
Difficulty breathing, grunting, very fast breathing, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
A seizure (fit), or a bulging soft spot on the head
urgentFlags: A temperature of 39C (102.2F) or higher in a baby aged 3 to 6 months
Not feeding, or feeding much less than usual
Fewer wet nappies, or no wet nappy for 8 hours or more
Vomiting repeatedly, or green vomit
Fever with a rash, or a fever that lasts 5 days or more
You feel something is seriously wrong

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds and other viruses are the most common cause, but young babies need checking to rule out serious infection.

commonCauses.title: Vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: A mild temperature after vaccinations is common; some vaccines can cause fever within 48 hours.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infections
commonCauses.detail: Urine infections, chest infections, sepsis or meningitis are less common but serious in young babies.

selfCare: Get medical help straight away if your baby is under 3 months and has a temperature of 38C or higher
Keep offering breast or formula milk little and often
Dress your baby in light clothing; do not wrap them up or bundle them in blankets
Paracetamol can be given from 2 months and ibuprofen from 3 months (if over 5kg), following the pack instructions; check with a pharmacist or doctor first for young babies
Check on your baby regularly during the night
avoid: Sponging your baby with cold water or giving cold baths
Giving aspirin to a baby or child under 16
Giving paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time, unless a doctor advises it
Waiting to see if a fever in a baby under 3 months settles
seeDoctorIf: Your baby seems unwell or not their usual self, even without a high temperature
Your baby has had a temperature after vaccination for more than 48 hours
You are worried about your baby

name: Fever in a child
summary: A high temperature is very common in children and is usually caused by a viral infection that the body can fight off. Watch how your child is behaving as well as the number on the thermometer.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
Pale, blue, grey or blotchy skin, lips or tongue (on darker skin, check the palms, soles and inside the lips)
Floppy, unresponsive, very drowsy or hard to wake
Difficulty breathing, grunting, or skin sucking in under the ribs
A stiff neck or pain looking at bright lights
A seizure (fit) for the first time
A weak, high-pitched or continuous cry
urgentFlags: A temperature that lasts 5 days or more
Not drinking, or signs of dehydration such as a dry mouth, no tears or peeing much less
Your child is getting worse, or you are worried
A fever with ear pain, pain when peeing, or a sore throat with white spots
A fever in a child with a long-term condition or weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu and other viruses are the most common cause and get better on their own.

commonCauses.title: Ear, throat or urine infections
commonCauses.detail: Some may need antibiotics.

commonCauses.title: Childhood illnesses
commonCauses.detail: Chickenpox, hand, foot and mouth disease, and scarlet fever often start with a fever.

commonCauses.title: Vaccinations
commonCauses.detail: A mild temperature after vaccines is common and usually settles within 48 hours.

selfCare: Give plenty of fluids, and breast or formula milk for babies
Look out for signs of dehydration
Give food if your child wants it
Use children's paracetamol or ibuprofen if your child is distressed, following the pack instructions for their age; do not give ibuprofen if they have chickenpox
Check on your child regularly during the night and keep them off nursery or school while they have a temperature
avoid: Undressing your child completely, sponging with cold water, or over-wrapping them
Giving aspirin to anyone under 16
Giving paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time, unless a doctor advises it
seeDoctorIf: The temperature has lasted more than 3 days and your child is not improving
Your child keeps getting high temperatures
You are worried about your child

name: Fever in adults

commonCauses.title: Life changes
commonCauses.detail: Moving, retiring, bereavement, a break-up or becoming a parent or carer.

commonCauses.title: Health and mobility
commonCauses.detail: Illness, disability or hearing loss can make socialising harder.

commonCauses.title: Depression and social anxiety
commonCauses.detail: Can make it hard to reach out, and loneliness can worsen them.

commonCauses.title: Working from home or living alone
commonCauses.detail: Fewer day-to-day contacts.

selfCare: Reach out to one person: a call, message or short visit
Join a group, class, club or volunteering based on your interests
Spend time in shared spaces such as libraries, cafés or parks
Use befriending services or helplines
Look after sleep and stay active
avoid: Relying on alcohol to cope
Comparing yourself with others on social media
seeDoctorIf: Loneliness is affecting your mood, sleep or appetite
You think you may be depressed or anxious
Hearing loss or health problems are making it hard to socialise

name: Loss of appetite
summary: Losing your appetite for a few days is common during an illness, with stress or after starting a medicine. If it lasts or comes with weight loss, it should be checked.
redFlags: Not eating or drinking at all with confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
urgentFlags: Not being able to keep fluids down
Signs of dehydration such as very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes

commonCauses.title: Short-term illness
commonCauses.detail: Infections such as colds, flu or stomach bugs often reduce appetite for a few days.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or low mood
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain commonly affects appetite.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines can reduce appetite or change taste.

commonCauses.title: Longer-term conditions
commonCauses.detail: Thyroid, liver, kidney or bowel problems and some cancers can cause ongoing appetite loss.

selfCare: Eat small, frequent meals or snacks rather than large meals
Choose foods you enjoy and that are easy to eat
Keep drinking fluids even if you do not feel like eating
Light activity and fresh air can help stimulate appetite
avoid: Skipping fluids along with food
Appetite-boosting supplements sold online, which are often unproven
seeDoctorIf: Your appetite has not returned after 2 weeks
You are losing weight without trying
You also feel low, anxious or hopeless
You have other ongoing symptoms such as tiredness, pain or night sweats

name: Loss of smell or changed sense of smell
summary: Losing your sense of smell, or things smelling different, is common after colds, flu, COVID-19 and sinus problems. It often recovers on its own within weeks, but can sometimes take longer.
redFlags: Loss of smell after a head injury with clear fluid from the nose, severe headache or confusion
Loss of smell with sudden weakness, face drooping or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Loss of smell with nosebleeds or bloody discharge on one side
Loss of smell with a blocked nose on one side only and facial swelling

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: Viral infections commonly affect smell, which usually returns over weeks.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis and nasal polyps
commonCauses.detail: Swelling and growths can block smells reaching the top of the nose.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and other allergies can reduce your sense of smell.

commonCauses.title: Ageing, smoking and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Smell naturally weakens with age and can be affected by smoking and medicines.

commonCauses.title: Neurological conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, loss of smell can be an early sign of conditions such as Parkinson's disease.

selfCare: Try smell training: sniff a few strong scents, such as lemon, rose, clove and eucalyptus, twice a day for several months
Fit a smoke alarm and check use-by dates, since you may not smell burning or spoiled food
Treat any blocked nose with saline rinses
Stop smoking
avoid: Supplements or sprays that claim to restore smell without evidence
Overusing decongestant sprays
seeDoctorIf: Your sense of smell has not returned within 3 weeks
You have lost smell without a cold or other clear cause
Changes in smell are affecting your eating or mood

sources.label: NHS – Lost or changed sense of smell

name: Loss of taste or changed taste
summary: Changes in taste are often linked to a cold, a problem with smell, a medicine or a mouth problem. Most of what we think of as flavour comes from smell, so the two often change together.
redFlags: Sudden change in taste with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Taste change with facial weakness developing over a day or two
Unable to eat or drink enough because of taste changes

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: Usually linked to a loss of smell and recovers over weeks.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Many medicines, including some antibiotics and cancer treatments, can cause a metallic or bitter taste.

commonCauses.title: Mouth problems
commonCauses.detail: Gum disease, oral thrush, dry mouth and poor oral hygiene can affect taste.

commonCauses.title: Smoking and ageing
commonCauses.detail: Both can dull your sense of taste.

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems
commonCauses.detail: Bell's palsy or head injury can affect taste.

selfCare: Keep up good mouth hygiene, including brushing your tongue
Try foods with strong flavours, herbs and varied textures
Drink enough water to prevent a dry mouth
Stop smoking
avoid: Adding lots of extra salt or sugar to make food taste better
Stopping a prescribed medicine without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: Your taste has not returned within 3 weeks
You think a medicine is causing taste changes
Taste changes are affecting your appetite or weight

name: Low mood or feeling depressed
summary: Low mood often lifts after a few days or weeks, especially with support. If you have felt low or lost interest in things for 2 weeks or more, it could be depression, which is common and treatable.
redFlags: Thoughts of ending your life, or making plans to
You have harmed yourself or feel you cannot keep yourself safe
You feel you are in immediate danger
urgentFlags: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm, even without a plan
Not eating or drinking, or unable to look after yourself
Seeing or hearing things others do not, or very unusual beliefs

commonCauses.title: Life events
commonCauses.detail: Loss, relationship problems, money worries, illness or loneliness.

commonCauses.title: Depression
commonCauses.detail: Persistent low mood or loss of interest for at least 2 weeks, often with poor sleep, appetite changes and tiredness.

commonCauses.title: After having a baby
commonCauses.detail: Postnatal depression can affect parents in the year after birth.

commonCauses.title: Seasonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Some people feel lower in the darker winter months.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs and health conditions
commonCauses.detail: These can cause or worsen low mood.

selfCare: Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling
Try to stay active, even with a short daily walk
Keep a routine with regular meals and sleep
Set small, achievable goals each day
Try evidence-based self-help such as CBT-based books or online programmes
avoid: Using alcohol or drugs to cope
Withdrawing from friends and family completely
Stopping prescribed antidepressants suddenly without advice
seeDoctorIf: You have felt low or lost interest in things for more than 2 weeks
Low mood is affecting work, relationships or daily life
Self-help is not working
You feel low after having a baby

sources.label: NHS – Low mood, sadness and depression

name: Lump in the groin or tummy (hernia)
summary: A soft lump in the groin or near the belly button that gets bigger when you cough or strain is often a hernia. Most are not urgent but should be checked.
redFlags: A hernia or groin lump that is suddenly very painful, hard or cannot be pushed back
A painful lump with vomiting and being unable to poo or pass wind
A lump that has turned red, purple or dark
urgentFlags: A groin lump with a high temperature and tenderness
A lump that is becoming more painful
A painful lump or swelling in the scrotum

commonCauses.title: Inguinal hernia
commonCauses.detail: Part of the bowel or fat pushes through a weak spot in the groin; more common in men.

commonCauses.title: Umbilical or incisional hernia
commonCauses.detail: A bulge at the belly button or near a previous operation scar.

commonCauses.title: Swollen lymph glands
commonCauses.detail: Glands in the groin can swell with an infection in the leg, foot or genitals.

commonCauses.title: Skin lumps
commonCauses.detail: Cysts or lipomas (fatty lumps) under the skin.

selfCare: Avoid heavy lifting and straining until the lump has been checked
Keep poo soft to avoid straining
Note whether the lump disappears when you lie down
avoid: Forcing a lump back in if it is painful
Relying on a support belt instead of getting it checked
seeDoctorIf: You have a new lump in your groin or tummy
A lump gets bigger over time
A lump causes discomfort when you lift, cough or strain

name: Lump or red or white patch in the mouth
aliases: sore in mouth that won't heal
summary: Most lumps and patches in the mouth are harmless, such as a bitten cheek or a blocked saliva gland. Any lump, ulcer or red or white patch that does not heal within 3 weeks should be checked by a dentist or doctor.
redFlags: A swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: A lump that is growing quickly
A lump with numbness of the lip or tongue
Bleeding from a lump or patch that does not stop easily

commonCauses.title: Minor injury
commonCauses.detail: Biting the cheek or lip can leave a lump that settles in a week or two.

commonCauses.title: Mucocele
commonCauses.detail: A harmless fluid-filled swelling, often on the lower lip, from a blocked saliva gland.

commonCauses.title: Gum boil from a tooth infection
commonCauses.detail: A small pus-filled lump on the gum near a painful tooth.

commonCauses.title: Leukoplakia or erythroplakia
commonCauses.detail: White or red patches that sometimes change into cancer.

commonCauses.title: Mouth cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common; risk is higher with smoking, chewing tobacco or betel, and heavy drinking.

selfCare: Keep your mouth clean and avoid irritating the area
Note when the lump or patch appeared and whether it changes
Stop smoking and cut down on alcohol
avoid: Picking at or trying to burst a lump
Waiting more than 3 weeks to get a non-healing lump or patch checked
seeDoctorIf: A lump, ulcer or patch has not healed within 3 weeks
A tooth has become loose for no clear reason
You have a lump in the neck as well
You have ongoing pain or difficulty swallowing

name: Lump or swelling in a testicle
summary: Most testicle lumps are harmless, such as cysts or swollen veins, but any new lump should be checked by a doctor because testicular cancer is easier to treat when found early.
redFlags: Sudden, severe testicle pain, especially with feeling or being sick
urgentFlags: A swollen, painful testicle with a high temperature
Swelling that gets bigger quickly

commonCauses.title: Epididymal cyst
commonCauses.detail: A smooth, fluid-filled lump above or behind the testicle; usually harmless.

commonCauses.title: Varicocele
commonCauses.detail: Swollen veins that feel like a 'bag of worms', more often on the left.

commonCauses.title: Hydrocele
commonCauses.detail: Fluid around the testicle causing painless swelling.

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Epididymitis or orchitis causes painful swelling.

commonCauses.title: Testicular cancer
commonCauses.detail: Usually a painless lump or hardening; most common in men aged 15 to 49.

selfCare: Check your testicles regularly, ideally after a warm bath or shower, so you know what is normal for you
Make an appointment even if the lump is painless
avoid: Waiting to see if a lump goes away
Squeezing or pressing hard on a lump
seeDoctorIf: You notice any new lump or swelling
A testicle has changed shape, size or feels harder
You have a heavy feeling in your scrotum

name: Memory problems or forgetfulness
summary: Everyone forgets things sometimes, and stress, poor sleep and low mood often make it worse. Memory problems that affect daily life should be checked, because some causes are treatable.
redFlags: Sudden confusion or memory loss that came on over minutes or hours
Memory loss with weakness, numbness, a drooping face or slurred speech
Memory loss after a head injury
Memory loss with a severe headache, high fever or stiff neck
urgentFlags: Memory or thinking getting noticeably worse over days to weeks
Memory problems with new unusual behaviour or personality change
Memory problems after starting a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and low mood
commonCauses.detail: Worry and depression make it hard to concentrate, which can feel like poor memory.

commonCauses.title: Poor sleep and tiredness
commonCauses.detail: Not sleeping well affects attention and memory.

commonCauses.title: Normal ageing
commonCauses.detail: Mild slowing of memory, such as forgetting names, is common with age.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, heavy drinking, an underactive thyroid or low vitamin B12 can affect memory.

commonCauses.title: Dementia
commonCauses.detail: Memory problems that steadily get worse and affect daily life can be an early sign of dementia.

selfCare: Use lists, a calendar, reminders and a fixed place for keys and glasses
Aim for regular, good-quality sleep
Stay physically active and socially connected
Cut down on alcohol
Ask someone who knows you well to help describe the changes to a doctor
avoid: Assuming memory problems are just old age without getting checked
Buying supplements or brain-training products that claim to prevent dementia
Stopping prescribed medicines without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: Memory problems are affecting your day-to-day life
Family or friends have noticed you are more forgetful
You are worried a relative is becoming increasingly forgetful
Memory is getting gradually worse

name: Migraine-type headache
summary: A migraine is usually a moderate or severe throbbing headache, often on one side, that can come with feeling sick and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people see flashing lights or zigzags (aura) beforehand.
redFlags: A headache that came on suddenly and is extremely painful
Weakness or inability to move an arm, leg or one side of the face
Problems speaking or remembering things
Loss of vision, or new blurred or double vision
Drowsiness or confusion
A seizure (fit)
Very high temperature with a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade
A recent head injury
urgentFlags: A migraine attack that has lasted longer than 72 hours
Aura symptoms lasting longer than 1 hour
A migraine during pregnancy or soon after having a baby
Aura symptoms happening for the first time without a headache

commonCauses.title: Migraine triggers
commonCauses.detail: Attacks can be set off by stress, tiredness, missed meals, dehydration, alcohol or changes in sleep.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Many women get migraines around their period, and patterns can change during pregnancy or menopause.

commonCauses.title: Environmental factors
commonCauses.detail: Bright or flickering lights, loud noise and strong smells can trigger attacks in some people.

commonCauses.title: Family history
commonCauses.detail: Migraine often runs in families, and some people are simply more prone to it.

selfCare: Lie down in a quiet, dark room at the start of an attack
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen as early as possible, following the pack instructions
Sip water, especially if you have been sick
Try a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on your forehead
Keep a diary to find and avoid your triggers, and keep regular meals and sleep
avoid: Using painkillers on many days each month, which can cause medication-overuse headache
Skipping meals or getting dehydrated
Unproven remedies sold as migraine cures
seeDoctorIf: Attacks are severe, getting worse, or lasting longer than usual
You have migraines more than once a week
Over-the-counter treatments are not controlling your symptoms
You regularly get migraines around your period
You have migraine with aura and are thinking about the combined contraceptive pill

name: Missed or irregular periods
summary: A late or missed period is often caused by pregnancy, stress, weight changes, exercise or contraception. Do a pregnancy test first if you could be pregnant.
redFlags: A missed period with sudden severe tummy pain, especially on one side
A missed period with shoulder-tip pain, fainting or dizziness
A positive pregnancy test with heavy bleeding and severe pain
urgentFlags: A positive pregnancy test with one-sided tummy pain or light bleeding
Being unable to keep food or fluids down

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: The most common reason if you have had sex; a home pregnancy test is accurate from the first day of a missed period.

commonCauses.title: Stress, weight loss or intense exercise
commonCauses.detail: These can stop or delay ovulation.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.detail: Pills, injections, implants and hormonal coils can make periods lighter, irregular or stop.

commonCauses.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome
commonCauses.detail: Irregular periods, sometimes with acne, extra hair growth or weight gain.

commonCauses.title: Menopause or thyroid problems
commonCauses.detail: Periods become irregular before the menopause; an over- or underactive thyroid can also affect them.

selfCare: Take a pregnancy test if you could be pregnant
Keep a record of your periods using a diary or app
Look after your wellbeing: eat regular balanced meals and manage stress where you can
avoid: Assuming you cannot get pregnant because your periods are irregular
Herbal products claimed to 'bring on' a period, which are unproven and may be unsafe
seeDoctorIf: You have missed 3 periods in a row and are not pregnant
You are under 45 and your periods have stopped
You are 15 or older and have not started your periods
Your periods are irregular and you are trying to get pregnant
You have bleeding after the menopause

name: Mood swings or extreme highs and lows
summary: Everyone's mood changes, but extreme highs (feeling very energetic, needing little sleep, racing thoughts) and lows that last days or weeks may be a sign of bipolar disorder or another condition that can be treated.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
Behaviour that puts you or others in immediate danger
Hearing voices or believing things that are clearly not true, with distress or risk
urgentFlags: Several days of very little sleep with racing thoughts and unusually high energy
Spending, driving or other behaviour that is out of character and risky
Very low mood after a period of feeling high

commonCauses.title: Stress, tiredness and life events
commonCauses.detail: Ordinary mood changes are often linked to these.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Periods, pregnancy and the menopause can affect mood.

commonCauses.title: Bipolar disorder
commonCauses.detail: Episodes of depression and mania or hypomania lasting days to weeks.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Can cause mood changes.

commonCauses.title: Personality disorders and ADHD
commonCauses.detail: Can involve rapid emotional changes.

selfCare: Keep a mood diary, including sleep, to spot patterns
Keep a regular routine for sleep, meals and activity
Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs
Ask someone close to tell you if they notice warning signs
avoid: Making big financial or life decisions when your mood is very high or low
Staying up all night
seeDoctorIf: Mood swings are affecting your life or relationships
You have periods of feeling unusually high or full of energy
You have had low mood for more than 2 weeks

name: Mouth ulcers
summary: Mouth ulcers are painful sores inside the mouth that are common and usually heal on their own within 1 to 2 weeks. An ulcer that lasts longer than 3 weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Mouth sores with a widespread rash, blistering skin or peeling, especially after a new medicine
Mouth swelling making it hard to breathe or swallow
urgentFlags: Unable to eat or drink because of pain, especially in a child
An ulcer that bleeds or becomes more painful, red and swollen
Many ulcers with a high temperature and feeling unwell

commonCauses.title: Minor injury
commonCauses.detail: Biting your cheek, sharp teeth, braces or dentures.

commonCauses.title: Stress, tiredness and hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Common triggers for recurring ulcers.

commonCauses.title: Certain foods or toothpastes
commonCauses.detail: Spicy or acidic foods, or toothpaste with sodium lauryl sulphate, can trigger ulcers.

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Such as hand, foot and mouth disease or cold sore virus.

commonCauses.title: Health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Low iron or vitamin B12, coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease can cause repeated ulcers.

selfCare: Use a soft toothbrush
Ask a pharmacist about pain-relieving gels, sprays or mouthwashes
Eat softer foods and drink cool drinks through a straw
Keep your mouth clean
avoid: Very spicy, salty, acidic or hard foods
Very hot drinks
Chewing gum
seeDoctorIf: An ulcer lasts longer than 3 weeks
An ulcer is different from ones you have had before, or near the back of the throat
You keep getting mouth ulcers
You also have ulcers elsewhere on the body, or painful, swollen joints

name: Muscle aches
summary: Aching muscles are usually caused by exercise, tension or a viral illness such as flu, and get better within a few days.
redFlags: Muscle aches with a high temperature, confusion, fast breathing or cold, blotchy skin
Muscle aches with a rash that does not fade when pressed under a glass
Severe muscle pain with very dark or brown pee
urgentFlags: Muscle pain with weakness, especially after starting a new medicine
Muscle aches with a tick bite and a spreading rash
Muscle pain with a stiff neck or severe headache

commonCauses.title: Exercise or overuse
commonCauses.detail: Delayed soreness 1 to 2 days after unaccustomed activity.

commonCauses.title: Viral illness
commonCauses.detail: Flu, COVID-19 and other viruses commonly cause body aches.

commonCauses.title: Stress and tension
commonCauses.detail: Tight muscles, especially in the neck and shoulders.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, such as statins, can cause muscle pain.

commonCauses.title: Long-term conditions
commonCauses.detail: Fibromyalgia, polymyalgia rheumatica, thyroid problems or low vitamin D.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids if you have a viral illness
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Use a warm bath or heat pack to ease aches
Gentle stretching and gradual return to exercise
avoid: Intense exercise while you have a fever
Stopping a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor
seeDoctorIf: Muscle aches last more than 2 weeks
You have muscle weakness
You are over 50 with new pain and stiffness in the shoulders and hips
You think a medicine is causing the pain

name: Muscle cramps
summary: Muscle cramps are sudden, painful tightening of a muscle, often in the calf at night. They are usually harmless and last a few minutes.
redFlags: Calf pain with swelling, warmth and redness and sudden breathlessness or chest pain
Severe muscle pain with very dark or brown pee and weakness
urgentFlags: Cramp-like calf pain with swelling, warmth or redness in one leg
Cramps with numbness, weakness or changes in sensation
Cramps after starting a new medicine, with muscle weakness or dark pee

commonCauses.title: Unknown cause
commonCauses.detail: Most night cramps have no clear cause and become more common with age.

commonCauses.title: Exercise and dehydration
commonCauses.detail: Overworked muscles and losing fluid through sweating.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Leg cramps are common in later pregnancy.

commonCauses.title: Medicines and medical conditions
commonCauses.detail: Diuretics, statins, nerve or kidney problems can cause cramps.

selfCare: Stretch and massage the muscle during a cramp, for example pulling your toes towards you for a calf cramp
Do regular calf stretches, especially before bed
Drink enough fluids during exercise and in hot weather
Paracetamol or ibuprofen can ease soreness afterwards, following the pack instructions
avoid: Quinine-containing tonic water as a treatment, which has little benefit
Unproven supplements sold for cramps
seeDoctorIf: Cramps happen often and disturb your sleep
Cramps last more than 10 minutes
You also have numbness, swelling or muscle weakness
You think a medicine is causing them

name: Nail changes
summary: Nail changes are common and are often caused by a fungal infection, injury or ageing. Some changes can be a sign of other health problems.
redFlags: Nails or fingertips that suddenly turn blue or grey, with difficulty breathing or feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Red, hot, swollen skin around a nail that is spreading, with a high temperature
A painful, pus-filled swelling next to a nail

commonCauses.title: Fungal nail infection
commonCauses.detail: Thickened, discoloured, brittle nails, more often on toenails.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Bruising under the nail or white marks after knocks.

commonCauses.title: Psoriasis or eczema
commonCauses.detail: Pitting, ridges or nails lifting from the nail bed.

commonCauses.title: Other health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Spoon-shaped nails can be linked to iron deficiency; clubbing can be linked to heart or lung problems.

commonCauses.title: Melanoma under the nail
commonCauses.detail: Rarely, a new dark streak that widens or spreads to the skin around the nail.

selfCare: Keep nails short, clean and dry
Wear well-fitting shoes and change socks daily
Ask a pharmacist about antifungal nail paints for mild fungal infections; treatment can take months
Moisturise brittle nails and wear gloves for wet work
avoid: Sharing nail clippers or towels
Cutting cuticles or picking at nails
seeDoctorIf: You notice a new dark streak or spot under a nail that was not caused by an injury
A nail infection has not improved with pharmacy treatment or is spreading
The shape of your nails changes, such as curving or clubbing
Nails are lifting off without a clear reason

name: Nappy rash
summary: Nappy rash is very common and causes red, sore patches in the nappy area. It usually clears in a few days with simple care and a barrier cream.
redFlags: A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it, with your baby seeming unwell
Your baby is floppy, very drowsy, or has a temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher under 3 months
urgentFlags: Blisters, open sores, pus or crusting in the nappy area
A rash with a high temperature
Bright red rash with spots spreading into the skin folds that is not improving

commonCauses.title: Irritation from wee and poo
commonCauses.detail: Skin in contact with a wet or dirty nappy for too long.

commonCauses.title: Fragranced products
commonCauses.detail: Soaps, bubble bath, lotions or wipes containing alcohol or perfume.

commonCauses.title: Thrush infection
commonCauses.detail: A bright red rash with spots, often in the skin folds; may need antifungal cream.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial infection
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, sores, blisters or crusts that need treatment.

selfCare: Change wet or dirty nappies as soon as possible
Clean the skin with water or fragrance-free, alcohol-free baby wipes, and pat dry
Leave the nappy off for as long as practical each day
Apply a thin layer of barrier cream at each change
Bath your baby daily, but not more than twice a day
avoid: Soap, bubble bath and lotions in the nappy area
Talcum powder
Tight nappies or clothing over the nappy area
Using steroid creams on a baby's nappy area unless a doctor advises it
seeDoctorIf: The rash has not cleared after a week of self-care
The rash keeps coming back
You think the rash may be thrush

name: Neck pain
summary: Neck pain and stiffness are common and usually caused by posture, sleeping awkwardly or muscle strain. They usually improve within a few weeks.
redFlags: A stiff neck with a high temperature and headache, sensitivity to light, or a rash that does not fade under a glass
Neck pain after a fall, car accident or blow to the head
Neck pain with weakness, numbness or loss of coordination in the arms or legs
Sudden severe neck pain with a sudden severe headache
urgentFlags: Neck pain with pins and needles or weakness in one arm
Neck pain with a high temperature and feeling unwell
Severe pain that is getting worse
A lump in the neck that is getting bigger

commonCauses.title: Posture and muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Working at a computer, looking down at a phone, or sleeping in an awkward position.

commonCauses.title: Wear and tear
commonCauses.detail: Age-related changes in the neck joints and discs.

commonCauses.title: Trapped nerve
commonCauses.detail: Pain spreading into the arm with tingling or numbness.

commonCauses.title: Whiplash
commonCauses.detail: Neck injury after a sudden jolt, such as in a car accident.

selfCare: Keep your neck moving gently; do not use a neck collar
Take ibuprofen or paracetamol, following the pack instructions
Use a heat pack or a cold pack for short periods
Use a low, firm pillow and check your posture at desks and screens
avoid: Wearing a neck collar unless advised by a doctor
Sudden, forceful neck movements or manipulation
Long periods looking down at screens
seeDoctorIf: Pain has not improved after a few weeks
Pain is severe or getting worse
You have pins and needles, numbness or weakness in your arms or hands
Pain is stopping you doing your normal activities

name: Needing to pee a lot
aliases: getting up at night to pee
summary: Needing to pee more often can be caused by drinking a lot, caffeine, an infection, an overactive bladder, prostate enlargement or diabetes. It is worth checking if it does not settle.
redFlags: Being very thirsty and peeing a lot with vomiting, stomach pain, deep or fast breathing, or confusion
Feeling very unwell with a high temperature, confusion or fast breathing
urgentFlags: Pain or burning when peeing, with a high temperature or pain in your back or side
Blood in your pee
Feeling very thirsty, tired and losing weight
Being unable to pee or only able to pass small amounts despite a strong urge

commonCauses.title: Drinking a lot, caffeine or alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Tea, coffee, energy drinks and alcohol make you pee more.

commonCauses.title: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.detail: Usually with burning and an urgent need to go.

commonCauses.title: Overactive bladder
commonCauses.detail: Sudden urges to pee, sometimes with leaking.

commonCauses.title: Enlarged prostate
commonCauses.detail: Common in older men, with a weak flow and getting up at night to pee.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes or pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: High blood sugar and pregnancy both cause more frequent peeing.

selfCare: Cut down on caffeine, fizzy drinks and alcohol
Drink normally through the day but less in the 2 hours before bed
Try bladder training, gradually lengthening the time between toilet visits
Do pelvic floor exercises if you also leak urine
avoid: Cutting down drastically on fluids, which can cause dehydration and concentrated, irritating urine

commonCauses.title: Anxiety

commonCauses.title: Trauma and PTSD

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and withdrawal

Cut down on alcohol and caffeine
Write down a recurring nightmare and imagine a different, calmer ending in the daytime

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: Swelling of the throat in anaphylaxis.

commonCauses.title: Throat infections
commonCauses.detail: Rare but serious infections such as epiglottitis.

Get medical help straight away

name: Nose injury or broken nose

commonCauses.title: Bruised nose
commonCauses.detail: Pain and swelling without broken bone; settles within a week or two.

commonCauses.title: Broken nose

commonCauses.title: Septal haematoma

Picking or blowing your nose until it has healed
Contact sports for at least 6 weeks

name: Nosebleed
summary: Nosebleeds are common and usually not serious. Most stop with simple first aid within 10 to 15 minutes.
redFlags: The nosebleed lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes despite pressure
The bleeding seems very heavy
Swallowing a large amount of blood that makes you vomit
The bleeding started after a blow to the head
Feeling weak, dizzy or faint

urgentFlags: A nosebleed in someone taking blood-thinning medicine

commonCauses.title: Picking or blowing the nose
commonCauses.detail: The blood vessels inside the front of the nose are delicate and easily damaged.

commonCauses.title: Dry air
commonCauses.detail: A dry nose from heating or changes in temperature cracks and bleeds more easily.

commonCauses.title: Colds and allergies

avoid: Tilting your head back, which makes you swallow blood
Lying down during a nosebleed
Picking or blowing your nose straight afterwards
seeDoctorIf: You have regular nosebleeds
A child under 2 has had a nosebleed
You have signs of anaemia such as tiredness, pale skin or breathlessness

name: Numbness or tingling in the face

redFlags: Sudden numbness or weakness on one side of the face, arm or leg
Face drooping on one side, or cannot smile evenly
Slurred or garbled speech, or difficulty understanding

commonCauses.title: Anxiety and fast breathing

commonCauses.title: Migraine

commonCauses.title: Dental work or dental problems

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems

commonCauses.title: Stroke or TIA

seeDoctorIf: Face numbness keeps coming back

name: Pain and stiffness in several joints
summary: Aching joints are common, especially with age or after a viral illness. Joints that are swollen, warm or stiff for more than 30 minutes in the morning should be checked.
redFlags: A single joint that is suddenly hot, red, very swollen and painful, with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A hot, red, swollen joint, especially if you cannot move it

Joint pain after a recent sexually transmitted infection, tummy upset or tick bite

commonCauses.title: Osteoarthritis
commonCauses.detail: Pain and stiffness, usually in the knees, hips and hands, worse after activity.

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Aching joints during or after flu and other viruses, usually settling within a few weeks.

commonCauses.title: Rheumatoid or other inflammatory arthritis
commonCauses.detail: Swollen, warm joints with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning.

commonCauses.title: Gout
commonCauses.detail: Sudden, very painful, red, swollen joint, often the big toe.

commonCauses.title: Overuse
commonCauses.detail: Repetitive movements at work or in sport.

Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, or use an anti-inflammatory gel, following the pack instructions

Supplements such as glucosamine or magnetic bracelets, which have little evidence of benefit
seeDoctorIf: Joint pain has lasted more than 2 weeks
Your joints are swollen or stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking

name: Pain during sex
summary: Pain during or after sex is common and has many causes, including vaginal dryness, infections and endometriosis. It is worth seeing a doctor, as most causes can be treated.

urgentFlags: Pain with a high temperature or unusual discharge
Bleeding after sex with pelvic pain
Painful sores or blisters on the genitals
