commonCauses.detail: A red, itchy rash where the skin touched something irritating or that you are allergic to.

commonCauses.title: Eczema
commonCauses.detail: Dry, itchy, cracked patches that come and go.

commonCauses.title: Hives
commonCauses.detail: Raised, itchy welts that move around and fade within a day.

commonCauses.title: Viral infection
commonCauses.detail: Many viruses cause a widespread blotchy rash with mild illness.

commonCauses.title: Psoriasis or fungal infection
commonCauses.detail: Scaly patches, or a ring-shaped itchy rash.

selfCare: Avoid anything you think might be irritating your skin
Use a plain moisturiser (emollient) and mild, unperfumed soap
Cool compresses can soothe itching
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines or mild steroid creams for itchy rashes
avoid: Scratching, which can cause infection
Hot baths and perfumed products
Strong steroid creams on the face or for long periods without advice
seeDoctorIf: A rash has not improved after 2 weeks
A rash keeps coming back
You are worried about a rash, or self-care has not helped
A rash is affecting your sleep or daily life

name: Sleepwalking or sleep talking
summary: Sleepwalking is when someone walks or does things while still asleep. It is common in children, usually harmless, and most grow out of it.
redFlags: Someone has been seriously injured while sleepwalking
Jerking, stiffening or tongue biting during sleep that may be a seizure
urgentFlags: Sleepwalking that puts the person or others at risk, such as leaving the house or using a car
Violent behaviour during sleep

commonCauses.title: Childhood development
commonCauses.detail: Common in children and often runs in families.

commonCauses.title: Lack of sleep and stress
commonCauses.detail: Overtiredness and anxiety make episodes more likely.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Including some sleeping tablets.

commonCauses.title: Other sleep problems
commonCauses.detail: Sleep apnoea or restless legs can trigger episodes.

selfCare: Keep regular sleep times and get enough sleep
Make the home safe: lock doors and windows and remove trip hazards
Gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed
Reduce stress and avoid alcohol before bed
avoid: Waking a sleepwalker suddenly
Sleeping on a top bunk or near stairs if you sleepwalk
seeDoctorIf: Sleepwalking happens often
It starts for the first time in adulthood
It causes injury or is disturbing others

name: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking
summary: Sudden slurred speech or difficulty finding or understanding words can be a sign of a stroke and needs emergency help. Speech that changes slowly over time should also be checked.
redFlags: Speech has suddenly become slurred, garbled or difficult to understand
Sudden difficulty finding words or understanding others
Speech problems with face drooping or weakness in an arm or leg
Speech problems with sudden confusion, severe headache or loss of balance
urgentFlags: Speech problems that came on suddenly but have now completely gone
Slurred speech after a head injury that has improved

commonCauses.title: Stroke or TIA (mini-stroke)
commonCauses.detail: Sudden speech problems are a key warning sign; a TIA can pass quickly but still needs urgent assessment.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, drugs or medicines
commonCauses.detail: Intoxication and some medicines can cause slurred speech.

commonCauses.title: Severe tiredness or migraine
commonCauses.detail: Some migraines and extreme tiredness can affect speech briefly.

commonCauses.title: Nerve and muscle conditions
commonCauses.detail: Gradual speech changes can come from conditions such as Parkinson's disease or motor neurone disease.

selfCare: Use the FAST check: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call emergency services
Note the time the speech problem started; this matters for treatment
Stay with the person until help arrives
avoid: Waiting to see if it gets better
Giving the person food or drink if they have trouble swallowing
Assuming slurred speech is just drunkenness without checking for other signs
seeDoctorIf: Speech has changed gradually over weeks or months
You have a hoarse or weak voice that is getting worse
You have difficulty swallowing as well as speech changes

name: Snoring
summary: Snoring is very common and often harmless, but loud snoring with pauses in breathing or gasping can be a sign of sleep apnoea. Lifestyle changes often help.
redFlags: Someone cannot be woken, or is struggling to breathe while asleep
Snoring with choking that does not settle when the person wakes
urgentFlags: Being so sleepy during the day that you have nearly fallen asleep while driving

commonCauses.title: Being overweight
commonCauses.detail: Extra weight around the neck narrows the airway.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and sleeping tablets
commonCauses.detail: Relax the throat muscles.

commonCauses.title: Sleeping on your back
commonCauses.detail: The tongue and soft tissues fall back.

commonCauses.title: Blocked nose
commonCauses.detail: Colds, allergies or nasal problems.

commonCauses.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea
commonCauses.detail: The airway repeatedly closes during sleep, causing pauses in breathing and gasping.

selfCare: Lose weight if you are overweight
Sleep on your side
Avoid alcohol for a few hours before bed
Stop smoking
Treat a blocked nose, for example with saline sprays
avoid: Sleeping tablets
Expensive anti-snoring devices before getting checked for sleep apnoea if you are very sleepy
seeDoctorIf: Someone has noticed you stop breathing, gasp or choke in your sleep
You feel very tired during the day
Snoring is affecting your life or your partner's sleep
Lifestyle changes have not helped

name: Sore or burning tongue
summary: A sore tongue is often caused by biting or burning it, a mouth ulcer or irritation from food. It usually heals within a few days.
redFlags: Sudden swelling of the tongue, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing or swallowing
urgentFlags: Tongue pain with difficulty swallowing or speaking
A sore tongue with a high temperature and feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Injury or burns
commonCauses.detail: Biting the tongue or hot food and drink; should heal within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Mouth ulcers
commonCauses.detail: Painful sores can appear on the tongue.

commonCauses.title: Geographic tongue
commonCauses.detail: Harmless map-like smooth patches that can feel sore with some foods.

commonCauses.title: Low iron, vitamin B12 or folate
commonCauses.detail: Can make the tongue smooth, red and sore.

commonCauses.title: Burning mouth syndrome
commonCauses.detail: An ongoing burning feeling with no visible cause, more common after the menopause.

selfCare: Eat soft, cool foods and drink through a straw
Rinse with salt water (adults only) or ask a pharmacist about pain-relieving gels
Keep your mouth clean with gentle brushing
Sip cold water or suck ice chips
avoid: Spicy, acidic or very hot foods and drinks
Smoking and alcohol
seeDoctorIf: Tongue pain or itchiness does not go away or gets worse
You have white or red patches on your tongue
A sore or lump on the tongue lasts longer than 3 weeks

name: Sore throat
summary: A sore throat is very common and is usually caused by a virus such as a cold or flu. It typically gets better on its own within a week.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing
Unable to swallow, or drooling because you cannot swallow saliva
A high-pitched noise when breathing in (stridor)
Severe symptoms that are getting worse quickly
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat
urgentFlags: A very high temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
Signs of dehydration, such as peeing less or dark urine
A weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or uncontrolled diabetes
Severe pain on one side of the throat with difficulty opening the mouth or a muffled voice

commonCauses.title: Viral infections
commonCauses.detail: Colds, flu and COVID-19 are the most common causes; antibiotics do not help.

commonCauses.title: Tonsillitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed tonsils, usually viral but sometimes bacterial, such as strep throat.

commonCauses.title: Glandular fever
commonCauses.detail: A viral infection causing a severe sore throat, swollen glands and tiredness, mostly in young people.

commonCauses.title: Irritation
commonCauses.detail: Smoking, dry air, acid reflux and shouting can make the throat sore.

selfCare: Gargle with warm salty water (adults only)
Drink plenty of fluids, and try cool or soft foods
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Suck ice cubes, ice lollies or lozenges (not for young children)
Rest, and ask a pharmacist whether you need further treatment
avoid: Expecting antibiotics for a viral sore throat
Smoking or smoky places
Very hot drinks that can scald the throat
seeDoctorIf: Your sore throat has not improved after a week
You often get sore throats
You have a sore throat with a lump in your mouth or neck
A child under 5 needs help for a sore throat

name: Sore, dry or cracked lips
summary: Dry, sore or cracked lips are very common and are usually caused by cold weather, wind, sun or licking your lips. They usually get better with simple care.
redFlags: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: Lips that are hot, painful and swollen, which could be an infection
Sore lips with mouth blisters, a rash and feeling unwell after a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Weather and dryness
commonCauses.detail: Cold, wind, dry air and sun dry out the lips.

commonCauses.title: Licking or biting the lips
commonCauses.detail: Saliva dries the lips further.

commonCauses.title: Angular cheilitis
commonCauses.detail: Sore, cracked corners of the mouth, sometimes from an infection or poorly fitting dentures.

commonCauses.title: Irritation or allergy
commonCauses.detail: Lipsticks, toothpaste or some foods can irritate the lips.

commonCauses.title: Dehydration and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Not drinking enough, and acne or other medicines, can dry the lips.

selfCare: Use a lip balm, ideally with sun protection
Drink plenty of fluids
Ask a pharmacist about creams for sore corners of the mouth
Cover your lips with a scarf in cold, windy weather
avoid: Licking, biting or picking your lips
Lip products that sting or make things worse
Sharing lip balms or cups
seeDoctorIf: Your lips are not getting better after 2 weeks
Sore corners of the mouth keep coming back
A sore, lump or crust on the lip does not heal within 3 weeks

name: Sores, blisters or warts on the genitals
summary: Sores, blisters or lumps on the genitals are often caused by sexually transmitted infections such as herpes or genital warts. A sexual health clinic can diagnose and treat them.
redFlags: Rapidly spreading redness, swelling and severe pain in the genital area with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Painful sores that make it hard or impossible to pee
Sores with a high temperature, headache and feeling unwell
Genital sores during pregnancy, especially late pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Genital herpes
commonCauses.detail: Small painful blisters that burst to leave red, open sores; can come back.

commonCauses.title: Genital warts
commonCauses.detail: Painless small growths or lumps caused by HPV.

commonCauses.title: Syphilis
commonCauses.detail: A usually painless sore that heals on its own, but the infection remains and needs treatment.

commonCauses.title: Skin causes
commonCauses.detail: Ingrown hairs, spots, cysts or friction can also cause bumps.

selfCare: Get checked at a sexual health clinic
Keep the area clean and dry
Use paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions
Bathing in salt water or applying petroleum jelly can ease herpes pain
avoid: Sex, including oral sex, until you have been checked or the sores have healed
Over-the-counter wart treatments meant for hands or feet on the genitals
Touching or picking the sores
seeDoctorIf: You have any new sore, blister or lump on the genitals
A partner has been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection
Sores keep coming back

name: Sprained or twisted ankle
summary: Sprains and strains are injuries to ligaments and muscles, often in the ankle, wrist or knee. Most get better within a few weeks with rest and gradual return to activity.
redFlags: A joint or bone that looks deformed or is sticking through the skin
A foot or hand below the injury that is cold, pale, blue or numb
A crack or snap heard at the time of injury with severe pain
urgentFlags: Being unable to put weight on the leg or use the limb
Severe pain that is not eased by painkillers
Swelling and bruising that is getting much worse
Tenderness directly over a bone

commonCauses.title: Ligament sprain
commonCauses.detail: Overstretching or tearing of a ligament, most often by rolling the ankle.

commonCauses.title: Muscle strain
commonCauses.detail: Overstretching or tearing of muscle fibres during sport or lifting.

commonCauses.title: Broken bone
commonCauses.detail: Can look similar to a sprain; severe pain, being unable to bear weight or tenderness over the bone suggest a fracture.

selfCare: Rest the injured area for the first 2 to 3 days
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours
Raise the injured area on a pillow as often as you can
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Start gentle movement after 2 to 3 days and build up gradually
avoid: Heat, alcohol, running and massage for the first 3 days
Putting ice directly on the skin
Returning to sport too quickly
seeDoctorIf: The injury has not improved after a week of self-care
The joint keeps giving way
Pain or swelling is getting worse after the first few days

name: Sticky eye or eye discharge
summary: A sticky or crusty eye is most often caused by conjunctivitis, which usually clears up on its own within 1 to 2 weeks. A newborn with sticky eyes, or eye discharge with pain or vision changes, needs checking.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision or severe eye pain
Swollen, red, hot skin around the eye with fever or difficulty moving the eye
Blood or pus coming from the eye after an injury
urgentFlags: A baby under 30 days old has a red, sticky eye
Pain in the eye or sensitivity to light
Changes in vision, such as wavy lines or flashing
A very red eye, or discharge while wearing contact lenses

commonCauses.title: Bacterial or viral conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Red eye with sticky yellow or watery discharge; it spreads easily.

commonCauses.title: Blocked tear duct
commonCauses.detail: Common in babies, causing a watery, sticky eye without much redness.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or a stye
commonCauses.detail: Eyelid inflammation can cause crusting and discharge.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Some STIs can cause conjunctivitis with heavy discharge.

selfCare: Clean crusts gently with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water, using a fresh piece for each eye
Wash your hands often and use your own towels and pillows
Ask a pharmacist for advice on eye drops
Stop wearing contact lenses until the eye has cleared
avoid: Rubbing the eye or touching it and then the other eye
Sharing towels, flannels or eye make-up
Using breast milk or home remedies in the eye
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms have not cleared up within 7 days
A baby has a sticky eye that does not settle
You wear contact lenses and have spots on your eyelids

sources.label: MedlinePlus – Eye burning, itching and discharge

name: Stomach ache
summary: Most stomach aches are caused by something minor such as indigestion, trapped wind or a stomach bug, and settle within a few days. Sudden, severe or persistent pain needs to be checked.
redFlags: Sudden, severe stomach pain that does not ease
Stomach pain with vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Black, sticky or bloody poo with stomach pain
Stomach that is hard and very tender to touch
Pain after a recent injury to the stomach area
Collapsing, fainting, or cold, clammy, pale or blue-tinged skin
Severe pain in early pregnancy or a possible pregnancy, especially on one side
urgentFlags: Pain that keeps getting worse or is still there after several hours
Pain that started around the belly button and moved to the lower right side
Stomach pain with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
Pain with being unable to keep any fluids down
Pain when passing urine or a need to pee much more often
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes

commonCauses.title: Indigestion or trapped wind
commonCauses.detail: Often linked to eating, rich or fatty food, or swallowing air, and usually eases on its own.

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug (gastroenteritis)
commonCauses.detail: Cramping pain with diarrhoea or vomiting that usually gets better within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: Cramps and bloating when poo is hard or infrequent.

commonCauses.title: Period pain or other pelvic causes
commonCauses.detail: Low cramping pain linked to the menstrual cycle.

commonCauses.title: Conditions needing treatment
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, appendicitis, gallstones, a stomach ulcer or a urine infection can cause stomach pain.

selfCare: Rest and sip water or other fluids regularly
Eat small, plain meals and stop eating if it makes the pain worse
A hot water bottle or warm (not hot) pad on the stomach may ease cramping
Over-the-counter paracetamol can help, following the pack instructions
Cut down on alcohol, caffeine, fatty and spicy food until you feel better
avoid: Taking ibuprofen or aspirin for stomach pain unless a pharmacist or doctor has advised it, as they can irritate the stomach
Lying flat straight after eating if the pain feels like indigestion
Strong laxatives unless constipation is clearly the cause
seeDoctorIf: The pain keeps coming back
You have lost weight without trying
Your bowel habits have changed for more than a few weeks
You have difficulty swallowing
You are over 55 and have new, persistent indigestion or stomach pain

name: Stomach ache in a child
summary: Tummy aches are very common in children and are usually caused by constipation, wind, a stomach bug or worry. Severe or worsening pain needs to be checked.
redFlags: Severe pain that does not ease, or a hard, swollen tummy
Green vomit, or vomit with blood
Blood or redcurrant-jelly-like material in the poo with pain that comes and goes
Sudden pain in the testicles, groin or scrotum in a boy
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
urgentFlags: Pain that moves to the lower right side or is worse when walking or jumping
Pain with a high temperature
Pain when peeing or peeing more often
Pain with not drinking or signs of dehydration
Pain that keeps getting worse over several hours

commonCauses.title: Constipation
commonCauses.detail: One of the most common causes of tummy ache in children.

commonCauses.title: Stomach bugs
commonCauses.detail: With vomiting or diarrhoea.

commonCauses.title: Wind, colic or eating too much
commonCauses.detail: Usually mild and short-lived.

commonCauses.title: Worry or stress
commonCauses.detail: Tummy aches can happen with anxiety about school or other things.

commonCauses.title: Appendicitis or urine infection
commonCauses.detail: Less common but need treatment.

selfCare: Let your child rest and give small sips of water
Give children's paracetamol for pain, following the pack instructions for their age
A warm (not hot) water bottle wrapped in a towel can help
Offer plain food when they feel like eating
avoid: Aspirin for anyone under 16
Laxatives unless a doctor has advised them
Fatty or spicy food while the pain lasts
seeDoctorIf: Tummy aches keep coming back
Your child is not growing or gaining weight
Your child has ongoing constipation or diarrhoea
Pain is linked to worry or affecting school

name: Stress or feeling overwhelmed
summary: Stress is the body's reaction to feeling under pressure. Short-term stress is normal, but long-lasting stress can affect sleep, mood and physical health.

Chest pain or pressure that you are not sure is stress
urgentFlags: Feeling unable to cope at all or to look after yourself
Drinking or using drugs heavily to cope

commonCauses.title: Work or study pressure
commonCauses.detail: Heavy workloads, deadlines and job insecurity.

commonCauses.title: Money and housing worries
commonCauses.detail: Common long-term sources of stress.

commonCauses.title: Relationships and caring
commonCauses.detail: Family conflict or caring for someone.

commonCauses.title: Big life changes
commonCauses.detail: Moving, bereavement, illness or a new baby.

selfCare: Break problems into smaller steps and focus on what you can change
Be physically active and spend time outdoors
Talk to friends, family or a support line
Try breathing exercises, mindfulness or relaxation
Protect time for sleep and things you enjoy
avoid: Using alcohol, smoking or drugs to cope
Taking on more than you can manage
Cutting yourself off from others
seeDoctorIf: Stress is affecting your sleep, mood or health for more than a few weeks
Self-help is not helping
You have physical symptoms such as headaches or palpitations that worry you

name: Stye or lump on the eyelid
summary: A stye is a small, painful lump on or inside the eyelid caused by an infected eyelash follicle or gland. Most get better on their own within 1 to 2 weeks.
redFlags: Swelling and redness spreading around the eye with fever, eye pain on movement, or a bulging eye
Changes in vision with a swollen, red eyelid
urgentFlags: A stye that is very painful or swollen
A stye that affects your vision
Pus coming from the eye itself
Redness or swelling spreading to the rest of the eyelid or eye

commonCauses.title: Stye (hordeolum)
commonCauses.detail: A bacterial infection of an eyelash root or eyelid gland, causing a red, tender lump.

commonCauses.title: Chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A blocked eyelid gland causing a firmer, often painless lump that can last weeks.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or rosacea
commonCauses.detail: Long-term eyelid inflammation makes styes more likely.

selfCare: Hold a clean flannel soaked in warm water against the eye for 5 to 10 minutes, 3 or 4 times a day
Gently massage the lump afterwards
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Keep eyelids clean
avoid: Squeezing or bursting the stye
Wearing contact lenses or eye make-up until it has healed
Rubbing the eye
seeDoctorIf: The stye has not got better within a few weeks
You keep getting styes
A lump on the eyelid is growing or bleeding

name: Sudden confusion
summary: Sudden confusion, sometimes called delirium, is when someone quickly becomes unable to think clearly, pay attention or know where they are. It can have many causes and needs medical help straight away.
redFlags: Someone has suddenly become confused
Confusion with a drooping face, arm weakness or slurred speech
Confusion with a high or very low temperature, fast breathing or mottled, blue or very pale skin
Confusion after a head injury
Confusion with a severe headache, stiff neck or a rash that does not fade
Confusion in someone with diabetes who may have low blood sugar and is not improving after sugar
urgentFlags: Mild confusion that comes and goes in an older person, especially with a urine infection or new medicine
Confusion that has mostly settled but has not been explained

commonCauses.title: Infection
commonCauses.detail: Infections such as a urine or chest infection are a common cause of sudden confusion, especially in older people. Sepsis is a serious cause.

commonCauses.title: Stroke or head injury
commonCauses.detail: Problems with the brain itself can cause sudden confusion.

commonCauses.title: Low blood sugar, low oxygen or dehydration
commonCauses.detail: These can affect how the brain works.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol or drugs
commonCauses.detail: New medicines, too much alcohol, withdrawal or recreational drugs can cause confusion.

selfCare: Stay with the person and keep reassuring them
Tell them who you are and where they are, using simple words and short sentences
Make a note of any medicines they take to give to the medical team
If they have diabetes and are awake and able to swallow, give a sugary drink while waiting for help

Asking lots of questions while they are confused
Driving them to hospital yourself if they are very unwell; call an ambulance
seeDoctorIf: You or a relative have gradually become more forgetful or confused

You think a medicine is making someone confused

name: Sudden hearing loss

summary: Hearing loss that comes on over hours or a few days needs to be checked quickly, because some types are more treatable when treatment starts early. A blocked ear from wax or a cold is a common harmless cause.

Sudden hearing loss with severe vertigo and inability to walk
Hearing loss after a head injury
urgentFlags: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears without an obvious cause like a cold or wax
Sudden hearing loss with ringing or a feeling of fullness in the ear
Hearing loss after a loud bang or an injury to the ear

commonCauses.title: Earwax or a cold
commonCauses.detail: A blocked ear can cause sudden muffled hearing.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or perforated eardrum

commonCauses.title: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss

commonCauses.title: Inner ear conditions
commonCauses.detail: Ménière's disease or labyrinthitis can affect hearing and balance.

avoid: Assuming it is just wax and waiting several days
Putting objects or home remedies in the ear
seeDoctorIf: Hearing has not fully returned after a cold or ear infection
You keep getting episodes of reduced hearing

name: Sudden hot, swollen joint

A hot, swollen joint after recent joint surgery, an injection or with an artificial joint, and feeling unwell
urgentFlags: A joint that is suddenly hot, red, swollen and very painful
Being unable to move the joint
A first episode of suspected gout

commonCauses.title: Gout
commonCauses.detail: Uric acid crystals cause sudden, severe pain, often in the big toe, foot, ankle or knee.

commonCauses.title: Septic arthritis
commonCauses.detail: A joint infection, which is a medical emergency.

commonCauses.title: Pseudogout
commonCauses.detail: Crystals of a different type, often in the knee of older people.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Bleeding into the joint after a knock or twist.

Rest and raise the joint
Keep it cool with a cold pack wrapped in a towel
Drink plenty of water
avoid: Alcohol, especially beer, and large amounts of red meat, offal or seafood if you have gout

Aspirin for gout pain
seeDoctorIf: You have had gout attacks before and they are becoming more frequent
Swelling has not gone down after treatment
You have lumps on your joints or ears

name: Sudden loss of vision
summary: Losing some or all of the sight in one or both eyes suddenly is an emergency, even if it comes back. Quick treatment can save sight and may reveal a stroke risk.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes, even if it has come back
A dark curtain or shadow moving across your vision
Sudden severe eye pain with vision loss
Vision loss with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Vision loss with a new headache and jaw pain or scalp tenderness
urgentFlags: Vision that is gradually getting worse over days
Patchy vision or blind spots that are new

commonCauses.title: Retinal detachment
commonCauses.detail: Often starts with flashes and floaters followed by a shadow over the vision.

commonCauses.title: Blocked blood vessel in the eye or stroke
commonCauses.detail: Can cause sudden painless loss of sight in one eye.

commonCauses.title: Giant cell arteritis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed arteries, usually in people over 50, with headache and scalp tenderness.

commonCauses.title: Acute glaucoma or other eye conditions
commonCauses.detail: Can cause a painful red eye and blurred vision.

selfCare: Get emergency help straight away; note the time it started

avoid: Waiting to see if vision returns
Rubbing or pressing on the eye
seeDoctorIf: You notice gradual changes in your vision
You have not had an eye test in the last 2 years

name: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or face
summary: Sudden swelling of the lips, tongue or face is often caused by an allergic reaction. If it affects breathing or swallowing it can be life-threatening (anaphylaxis) and needs emergency help.
redFlags: Lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swelling
Breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, wheezing, choking or gasping
Throat feels tight or struggling to swallow
Skin, tongue or lips turning blue, grey or pale
Suddenly very confused, drowsy or dizzy, or fainting
urgentFlags: Swelling of another part of the body, such as the hands or feet, that came on suddenly
Mild lip swelling that keeps coming back
Swelling that started after a new medicine

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: To foods such as nuts or shellfish, insect stings, latex or medicines.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors) can cause swelling, even after years of use.

commonCauses.title: Hereditary angioedema
commonCauses.detail: A rare inherited condition causing repeated swelling.

commonCauses.title: Local injury or infection
commonCauses.detail: A bite, burn or infection can cause swelling of one area.

Keep a note of anything you ate, touched or took before the swelling
avoid: Waiting to see if swelling of the tongue or throat gets better
Standing or walking about during a severe reaction
Taking the suspected trigger again
seeDoctorIf: You have had swelling and do not know the cause
Swelling keeps coming back
You think a regular medicine may be causing it

name: Sunburn
summary: Sunburn makes the skin red, hot, sore and sometimes blistered, and usually improves within a week. Severe sunburn or heat illness needs medical help.
redFlags: Confusion, fainting, seizures or loss of consciousness
A temperature of 40C (104F) or higher with hot skin that has stopped sweating
Fast breathing or breathlessness with feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Large areas of blistering or swelling
Sunburn with a high temperature, chills, headache, dizziness or feeling sick
Sunburn in a baby or young child
Signs of dehydration such as very dark pee or not peeing

commonCauses.title: Too much UV exposure
commonCauses.detail: From the sun or sunbeds, especially between 11am and 3pm and near water or snow.

commonCauses.title: Not enough sun protection
commonCauses.detail: Missed areas, too little sunscreen or not reapplying after swimming.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines make skin more sensitive to sunlight.

selfCare: Get out of the sun and cool the skin with a cool shower, bath or damp towel
Apply aftersun or an unperfumed moisturiser
Drink plenty of water
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain, following the pack instructions
avoid: Further sun exposure until the skin has healed
Popping blisters or picking peeling skin
Putting ice, butter or petroleum jelly on sunburnt skin
seeDoctorIf: Sunburn has not improved after a week
You keep getting sunburnt easily despite protection
You notice changes in moles afterwards

name: Swollen ankles, feet or legs
summary: Swelling in the ankles, feet and legs is often caused by fluid building up from standing or sitting for a long time, hot weather or pregnancy. It usually goes away on its own.
redFlags: Swelling with sudden breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood
Swelling in one leg with chest pain or breathlessness
Swelling with a sudden severe headache, vision changes or pain under the ribs in pregnancy
urgentFlags: Swelling in one leg only, especially with pain, warmth or redness in the calf
Swelling that is getting worse quickly
Swelling with breathlessness when lying down or doing light activity
Swelling with red, hot, painful skin or a high temperature
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet in pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Standing or sitting for long periods
commonCauses.detail: Including long flights; fluid collects in the legs.

commonCauses.title: Hot weather or pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Mild swelling is very common in both.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some blood pressure medicines, steroids and anti-inflammatories cause swelling.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: A sprain or strain causes swelling around the injured area.

commonCauses.title: Heart, kidney, liver or vein problems, or a blood clot
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes that need assessment.

selfCare: Raise your legs on a pillow when lying down
Walk regularly to improve blood flow
Wear wide, comfortable shoes
Avoid sitting or standing still for long periods
avoid: Wearing tight clothing or socks that leave marks
Sitting with your legs crossed for long periods
Diuretic ('water') tablets or herbal products without medical advice
seeDoctorIf: Swelling has not improved after 3 days of self-care
Swelling keeps coming back
You have heart, kidney or liver disease
Skin over the swelling is changing colour or becoming tight and shiny

name: Swollen face or gum from a tooth (dental abscess)
summary: A dental abscess is a build-up of pus from an infection in a tooth or gum. It causes intense pain and swelling and will not go away on its own, so it needs urgent dental treatment.
redFlags: Finding it hard to breathe, speak or swallow
A swollen or painful eye, or sudden problems with eyesight
A lot of swelling in the mouth or neck
Finding it hard to open your mouth
Feeling very unwell with a high temperature, fast heartbeat or confusion
urgentFlags: You think you have a dental abscess
Intense toothache with a swollen face or jaw
A bad taste in the mouth with pain and swelling

commonCauses.title: Untreated tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Bacteria reach the nerve and cause infection at the root.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease
commonCauses.detail: Infection can form a pocket of pus in the gum.

commonCauses.title: Cracked or damaged tooth
commonCauses.detail: Lets bacteria into the inner tooth.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Eat soft foods and use a soft toothbrush
Avoid very hot or cold food and drink
Contact a dentist urgently, or emergency dental services if closed
avoid: Squeezing or bursting the swelling yourself
Waiting for it to go away; antibiotics alone do not cure an abscess
Using leftover antibiotics
seeDoctorIf: Any suspected abscess, even if the pain eases (the infection can remain)
Pain or swelling returns after treatment

name: Swollen glands in the neck
summary: Swollen glands (lymph nodes) in the neck are usually a sign your body is fighting an infection such as a cold or sore throat. They normally go down within about 2 weeks.
redFlags: Swollen glands with difficulty breathing
Swollen neck with a very sore throat and inability to swallow saliva or drooling
A rapidly spreading red, hot swelling of the neck with fever
urgentFlags: Swollen glands and finding it very difficult to swallow
Swollen glands with a very high temperature and feeling very unwell

commonCauses.title: Colds and throat infections
commonCauses.detail: The most common reason glands swell; they shrink as the infection clears.

commonCauses.title: Ear, tooth or skin infections
commonCauses.detail: Infections near the neck often cause nearby glands to swell.

commonCauses.title: Glandular fever and other viruses
commonCauses.detail: Can cause swollen glands for several weeks.

commonCauses.title: Rarely, cancer
commonCauses.detail: Such as lymphoma or leukaemia, usually with hard, painless glands that keep growing.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if they are sore, following the pack instructions
Treat the underlying cold or sore throat
avoid: Squeezing or massaging a swollen gland
Ignoring a lump that keeps growing
seeDoctorIf: The glands are getting bigger or have not gone down after a week or two
They feel hard or do not move when you press them
You have night sweats or unexplained weight loss
You have no other signs of infection
The swelling is just above or below the collarbone

name: Swollen or drooping eyelid
summary: A swollen eyelid is often caused by an allergy, a stye, an insect bite or rubbing the eye. Swelling that is red, hot and painful, or that affects vision, needs to be seen quickly.
redFlags: Swelling of the eyelids with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing
Red, swollen eyelid with fever, pain when moving the eye, a bulging eye or changes in vision
An eyelid that drooped suddenly with a severe headache, double vision, face drooping or weakness
urgentFlags: Your swollen eyelid is red, hot, painful, tender or blistered
Your eyelid droops suddenly
You cannot open your eye or keep it open
A newborn baby has a sticky, red, swollen eye

commonCauses.title: Allergy
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever, cosmetics or insect bites can cause puffy, itchy eyelids.

commonCauses.title: Stye or chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A lump on the eyelid with local swelling.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation of the eyelids or eye surface can cause swelling.

commonCauses.title: Fluid and sleep
commonCauses.detail: Puffy eyes in the morning are common and often linked to salt, alcohol or poor sleep.

commonCauses.title: Cellulitis around the eye
commonCauses.detail: A skin infection that needs urgent treatment, especially in children.

selfCare: Hold a cool compress over the closed eye
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines if allergy is likely
Keep the eyelids clean
Raise your head with an extra pillow at night
avoid: Rubbing or squeezing the eyelid
Wearing make-up or contact lenses until the swelling settles
Using a product you suspect caused a reaction
seeDoctorIf: Eyelid symptoms are not improving after a few days
You keep getting swollen eyelids
Your eyelid has gradually started to droop
You have yellow patches or lumps around your eyes

name: Teeth grinding or clenching
summary: Teeth grinding and jaw clenching often happen during sleep, and are linked to stress, anxiety, alcohol, caffeine and smoking. It can cause jaw pain, headaches and worn teeth.
redFlags: Jaw pain with chest pain, shortness of breath or sweating
urgentFlags: Jaw locking or being unable to open your mouth
A cracked or broken tooth with pain

commonCauses.title: Stress and anxiety
commonCauses.detail: The most common cause of grinding and clenching.

commonCauses.title: Sleep problems
commonCauses.detail: Grinding is linked to snoring and sleep apnoea.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol, caffeine, smoking and drugs
commonCauses.detail: These can make grinding worse.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Some antidepressants can cause grinding.

selfCare: Try ways to relax, such as breathing exercises, exercise or a calming bedtime routine
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening
Stop smoking
Practise keeping your lips together and teeth apart during the day
Apply a warm flannel to sore jaw muscles
avoid: Chewing gum or pens
Hard or chewy foods if your jaw is sore
seeDoctorIf: You grind your teeth and have tooth damage or sensitive teeth
You have pain in your jaw, face or ear
Your partner says you grind your teeth in your sleep
You are worried about your child grinding their teeth

name: Teething
summary: Teething can make babies sore, dribbly and unsettled, usually from around 6 months. Teething does not cause a high temperature or illness.
redFlags: A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher in a baby under 3 months
Floppy, unresponsive or very hard to wake
A rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
urgentFlags: A temperature of 39C (102.2F) or higher in a baby aged 3 to 6 months
Not feeding or drinking, or fewer wet nappies
Diarrhoea or vomiting, which are not caused by teething

commonCauses.title: Teeth coming through
commonCauses.detail: Red, swollen gums, drooling, chewing and being unsettled.

commonCauses.title: Other illnesses
commonCauses.detail: Fever, diarrhoea or a rash suggest an infection rather than teething.

selfCare: Give your baby a teething ring cooled in the fridge (not the freezer)
Gently rub the gums with a clean finger
From 6 months, offer healthy, sugar-free foods to chew, such as cold pieces of vegetable, and stay with them
Children's paracetamol or ibuprofen can be used from the right age if your baby is distressed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Amber teething necklaces or bracelets, which can cause choking or strangulation
Teething gels with local anaesthetic, such as benzocaine or lidocaine, for young babies unless a pharmacist advises
Frozen teething rings or sugary foods and drinks
seeDoctorIf: Your baby has symptoms of illness, such as a high temperature
No teeth have come through by 12 months
You are worried about your baby's teeth

name: Testicle pain
summary: Sudden, severe testicle pain can be testicular torsion, an emergency that needs surgery within hours. Milder pain is often due to an infection or injury.
redFlags: Sudden, severe pain in one testicle
Testicle pain with feeling sick or being sick
A testicle that is higher than usual or lying at an unusual angle
Severe pain after an injury to the testicles that does not ease within an hour
Severe pain, swelling and redness of the scrotum or groin with a high temperature and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: Pain and swelling that came on over a day or two
Testicle pain with a high temperature
Testicle pain with burning when peeing or discharge from the penis
Pain with swelling of the scrotum

commonCauses.title: Testicular torsion
commonCauses.detail: The testicle twists and cuts off its blood supply; most common in boys and young men, and needs emergency surgery.

commonCauses.title: Epididymitis or orchitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection or inflammation causing pain and swelling, sometimes linked to sexually transmitted infections or mumps.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: A blow to the testicles; pain should ease within an hour.

commonCauses.title: Varicocele or cyst
commonCauses.detail: Swollen veins or fluid-filled lumps can cause a dull ache.

commonCauses.title: Hernia or kidney stone
commonCauses.detail: Pain can spread to the testicles from the groin or kidneys.

selfCare: Get emergency help straight away for sudden severe pain
For mild pain, wear supportive underwear and rest
Take paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Use a cold pack wrapped in a towel for swelling after an injury
avoid: Waiting to see if sudden severe testicle pain goes away; torsion can damage the testicle within hours
Sex until an infection has been treated
seeDoctorIf: You have a dull ache in the testicles that keeps coming back
You notice a lump or change in the shape or feel of a testicle
Your scrotum feels heavy or swollen

name: Thoughts of suicide
summary: If you are having thoughts of ending your life, you are not alone and help is available right now. Talking to someone can help you get through this moment.
redFlags: You have made plans or have the means to end your life
You feel you cannot keep yourself safe right now
You have taken an overdose or seriously harmed yourself
You are worried someone else is about to act on suicidal thoughts
urgentFlags: You are having thoughts of suicide, even without a plan
Suicidal thoughts are becoming more frequent or stronger
You have recently stopped or changed mental health medicine and feel worse

commonCauses.title: Depression and other mental health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Feeling hopeless or trapped is a symptom that treatment can help.

commonCauses.title: Overwhelming life events
commonCauses.detail: Loss, relationship breakdown, debt, abuse or isolation.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol and drugs
commonCauses.detail: Can make thoughts stronger and actions more impulsive.

commonCauses.title: Long-term pain or illness
commonCauses.detail: Living with ongoing illness can feel overwhelming.

selfCare: Call your local emergency number (such as 911, 999 or 112) if you are in immediate danger
Contact a crisis line now, for example 988 in the US and Canada or Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland
Tell someone you trust how you are feeling and ask them to stay with you
Remove or move away from anything you could use to harm yourself
Make a safety plan listing people to call, reasons for living and safe places to go
avoid: Being alone if you feel unsafe
Drinking alcohol or using drugs
Making big decisions while you feel like this
seeDoctorIf: You have had suicidal thoughts recently, even if they have passed
You often feel hopeless or that others would be better off without you
You want help making a safety plan

name: Tiredness and fatigue
summary: Feeling tired is very common and is often linked to sleep, stress, diet or a recent illness. Tiredness that lasts weeks without a clear reason is worth checking.
redFlags: Sudden weakness or numbness on one side, a drooping face or slurred speech
Extreme tiredness with chest pain, severe breathlessness or fainting
Extreme drowsiness or confusion with a high temperature
Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life
urgentFlags: Tiredness with vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo
Tiredness with breathlessness, a racing heart or looking very pale
Tiredness with extreme thirst, peeing a lot and weight loss

commonCauses.title: Lifestyle
commonCauses.detail: Not enough sleep, irregular hours, alcohol, caffeine, too little or too much exercise.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or low mood
commonCauses.detail: Emotional strain and depression commonly cause exhaustion.

commonCauses.title: Recent infection
commonCauses.detail: Tiredness can last several weeks after viral illnesses such as flu or COVID-19.

commonCauses.title: Anaemia or thyroid problems
commonCauses.detail: Iron deficiency and an underactive thyroid are common, treatable causes.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes, sleep apnoea, chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), medicines, and less commonly cancer.

selfCare: Go to bed and get up at the same time every day
Eat regular, balanced meals and drink enough water
Be active every day, starting gently if needed
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening
Talk to someone or seek support if stress or worry is the cause
avoid: Energy drinks and large amounts of caffeine
Unproven 'energy-boosting' or 'adrenal fatigue' supplements
Napping for long periods during the day
seeDoctorIf: You have felt tired for several weeks without an obvious reason
Tiredness is affecting your daily life
You have also lost weight without trying
You have other symptoms such as heavy periods, night sweats or swollen glands
You snore loudly and stop breathing in your sleep

name: Toothache
summary: Toothache is usually caused by tooth decay, a cracked tooth, gum problems or an infection. It needs a dentist to find and treat the cause.
redFlags: Swelling around the eye or in the neck
Swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe, swallow or speak
Cannot open your mouth properly with spreading facial swelling and fever
urgentFlags: A swollen cheek or jaw
A high temperature with toothache
Pain when biting with red gums or a bad taste in the mouth
Severe pain that painkillers do not control

commonCauses.title: Tooth decay
commonCauses.detail: Cavities expose the sensitive inner part of the tooth.

commonCauses.title: Dental abscess
commonCauses.detail: A collection of pus from infection, causing throbbing pain and sometimes swelling.

commonCauses.title: Cracked tooth or damaged filling
commonCauses.detail: Pain often when biting or with hot and cold.

commonCauses.title: Gum disease or wisdom teeth
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed gums or an erupting wisdom tooth can cause pain.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Can cause aching in the upper back teeth.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Use a pain-relieving mouth gel from a pharmacy
Rinse with warm salt water (adults only)
Eat soft foods and chew on the other side
Contact a dentist; if your dentist is closed, ask about emergency dental services
avoid: Holding aspirin against the gum, which can burn it
Very hot, cold or sugary food and drink
Using painkillers for weeks instead of getting the tooth treated
seeDoctorIf: Toothache lasts more than 2 days
Painkillers do not help
The tooth is sensitive or painful when you bite

name: Tremor or shaking hands
summary: A slight tremor is normal and often becomes more noticeable with stress, tiredness, caffeine or cold. A tremor that is getting worse or affecting daily life should be checked.
redFlags: Shaking with sudden weakness, numbness, face drooping or slurred speech
Uncontrolled jerking of the body with loss of awareness (a possible seizure)
Shaking, sweating and confusion in someone with diabetes that does not improve after sugar
Shaking with high fever, confusion or difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: A new tremor that started after a new medicine
Tremor with a racing heartbeat, weight loss and feeling hot
Shaking during alcohol withdrawal

commonCauses.title: Normal (physiological) tremor
commonCauses.detail: Becomes more noticeable with stress, anxiety, tiredness, cold, caffeine or nicotine.

commonCauses.title: Essential tremor
commonCauses.detail: A common, often inherited tremor of the hands, typically when holding something or moving.

commonCauses.title: Medicines, alcohol and an overactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Some medicines, alcohol withdrawal and an overactive thyroid can cause shaking.

commonCauses.title: Parkinson's disease
commonCauses.detail: Usually a tremor at rest, often starting on one side, with slowness or stiffness.

selfCare: Cut down on caffeine
Try to manage stress and get enough sleep
Use heavier cups and cutlery, and hold items with both hands
Keep a note of when the tremor is worse
avoid: Using alcohol to calm a tremor
Stopping prescribed medicines without talking to a doctor
seeDoctorIf: The tremor is getting worse over time
It is affecting your daily activities
You have other symptoms such as stiffness, slowness or problems with balance
You think a medicine may be causing it

name: Unexplained weight gain or puffiness
summary: Weight gain is usually linked to diet, activity, medicines or life changes. Rapid weight gain with swelling, or with tiredness and feeling cold, should be checked.
redFlags: Rapid swelling with breathlessness, especially when lying down, or chest pain
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet in pregnancy with severe headache or vision problems
urgentFlags: Gaining a lot of weight over a few days with swollen legs or tummy
Puffiness with peeing much less than usual or foamy pee

commonCauses.title: Diet and activity
commonCauses.detail: Eating more or moving less than usual, including after stopping smoking.

commonCauses.title: Medicines
commonCauses.detail: Steroids, some antidepressants, diabetes medicines and others.

commonCauses.title: Underactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Weight gain with tiredness, feeling cold, constipation and dry skin.

commonCauses.title: Fluid retention
commonCauses.detail: Heart, kidney or liver problems can cause rapid weight gain from fluid.

commonCauses.title: Hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Menopause, polycystic ovary syndrome and, rarely, Cushing's syndrome.

selfCare: Keep a food and activity diary for a couple of weeks
Eat a balanced diet and be active most days
Weigh yourself once a week at the same time
avoid: Crash diets and unregulated weight-loss pills
Stopping a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor
seeDoctorIf: You are gaining weight without a clear reason
You also feel tired, cold or low
You have swelling in your legs or tummy
You think a medicine is causing it

name: Unexplained weight loss
summary: Losing weight without trying, especially 5% or more of your body weight over 6 to 12 months, should always be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Weight loss with vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like poo
Weight loss with extreme thirst, peeing a lot, vomiting, fast breathing or confusion
urgentFlags: Weight loss with difficulty swallowing
Weight loss with yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Weight loss with being very thirsty and peeing a lot

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety or depression
commonCauses.detail: Can reduce appetite and lead to weight loss.

commonCauses.title: Overactive thyroid
commonCauses.detail: Weight loss with a fast heartbeat, sweating and anxiety.

commonCauses.title: Diabetes
commonCauses.detail: Weight loss with thirst, peeing a lot and tiredness.

commonCauses.title: Digestive problems
commonCauses.detail: Coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease or other conditions that affect absorption.

commonCauses.title: Cancer or long-term infections
commonCauses.detail: Less common, but the reason unexplained weight loss needs checking.

selfCare: Weigh yourself and record it so you can show the doctor how much you have lost and over what time
Note any other symptoms such as changes in appetite, bowel habit, sweating or tiredness
Eat regular meals and snacks while waiting to be seen
avoid: Waiting to see if it stops
Assuming weight loss is due to stress without being checked
seeDoctorIf: You have lost weight without trying
You have also had a change in bowel habits, night sweats or tiredness
You have a lump anywhere in your body

name: Unusual vaginal discharge
summary: Some vaginal discharge is normal and changes during the cycle. A change in colour, smell or texture, or itching, is often due to thrush or bacterial vaginosis, which are easily treated.
redFlags: Discharge with severe tummy pain, a high temperature and feeling very unwell
Feeling faint, confused or very unwell with a high temperature and a tampon or menstrual cup in place
urgentFlags: Discharge with pelvic pain or a high temperature
Discharge with bleeding between periods or after sex
Unusual discharge during pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Bacterial vaginosis
commonCauses.detail: Thin, grey-white discharge with a strong fishy smell.

commonCauses.title: Thrush
commonCauses.detail: Thick, white discharge like cottage cheese, with itching and soreness.

commonCauses.title: Sexually transmitted infections
commonCauses.detail: Trichomoniasis, chlamydia or gonorrhoea can cause green, yellow or frothy discharge.

commonCauses.title: Normal changes
commonCauses.detail: Discharge changes with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, contraception and the menopause.

selfCare: Wash the outside of the vagina gently with water or plain unperfumed soap
Wear cotton underwear and avoid tight clothing
Ask a pharmacist about treatments for thrush or bacterial vaginosis if you have had it diagnosed before and recognise the symptoms
Use condoms with new or casual partners
avoid: Douching or washing inside the vagina
Perfumed soaps, wipes and feminine deodorants
Home remedies such as yoghurt, garlic or tea tree oil inside the vagina
seeDoctorIf: This is the first time you have had these symptoms
Treatment has not worked or symptoms keep coming back
You might have a sexually transmitted infection
You are pregnant, under 16 or have gone through the menopause

name: Unwanted intrusive thoughts
summary: Most people have unwanted or upsetting thoughts sometimes. When they cause a lot of distress or lead to repeated checking, cleaning or other rituals, it may be obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), which is treatable.
redFlags: Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself, with a wish or plan to act on them
You feel you cannot keep yourself or others safe
urgentFlags: Thoughts or rituals are stopping you eating, sleeping or leaving the house
Severe distress that you cannot manage

commonCauses.title: Normal intrusive thoughts
commonCauses.detail: Most people have them; they do not mean you want to act on them.

commonCauses.title: Obsessive compulsive disorder
commonCauses.detail: Obsessions cause anxiety, and compulsions are done to ease it.

commonCauses.title: Anxiety and stress
commonCauses.detail: Make unwanted thoughts more frequent and sticky.

commonCauses.title: After having a baby
commonCauses.detail: Upsetting thoughts about harm to the baby are common and treatable.

selfCare: Remind yourself that having a thought does not mean you want it or will act on it
Try not to push thoughts away or seek repeated reassurance, which can strengthen them
Use evidence-based self-help based on CBT
Be active and look after your sleep
avoid: Repeated checking, googling or seeking reassurance
Using alcohol or drugs to cope
seeDoctorIf: Thoughts or rituals take up more than an hour a day
They cause you a lot of distress
They are affecting work, relationships or daily life

name: Vertigo (spinning sensation)
summary: Vertigo is the feeling that you, or everything around you, is spinning. It is often caused by an inner ear problem and usually gets better without treatment.
redFlags: Vertigo with double vision or loss of vision
Vertigo with sudden hearing loss
Vertigo with trouble speaking
Vertigo with weakness, numbness or tingling in an arm or leg
Being unable to stand or walk at all
Someone with vertigo who cannot be woken up
urgentFlags: Vertigo with a severe headache
Vertigo with being sick or feeling very sick
Vertigo with a very high temperature or feeling hot and shivery

commonCauses.title: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
commonCauses.detail: Short bursts of spinning triggered by moving the head, such as rolling over in bed.

commonCauses.title: Labyrinthitis or vestibular neuritis
commonCauses.detail: Inner ear inflammation, often after a viral infection, causing vertigo that can last days.

commonCauses.title: Migraine
commonCauses.detail: Some people get vertigo as part of a migraine, sometimes without much headache.

commonCauses.title: Ménière's disease
commonCauses.detail: Attacks of vertigo with hearing loss, ringing and a feeling of fullness in one ear.

selfCare: Lie still in a quiet, dark room during an attack
Move your head slowly and carefully
Sit down straight away when you feel dizzy
Get up slowly in the morning and sit on the edge of the bed for a minute
Sleep with your head slightly raised on two or more pillows
avoid: Driving or using machinery while you have vertigo
Bending down or stretching up suddenly
Climbing ladders or working at heights
seeDoctorIf: Vertigo will not go away or keeps coming back
It is affecting your daily life
You have hearing changes or ringing in the ears
You have had a fall

name: Vomiting in adults
summary: Vomiting is usually caused by a stomach bug or food poisoning and stops within 1 to 2 days. The main risk is losing too much fluid.
redFlags: Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
Green vomit, or vomit that smells like poo
Sudden, severe stomach pain or a hard, swollen stomach
A stiff neck with pain when looking at bright lights
A sudden, severe headache
Confusion, extreme drowsiness or fainting
Signs of sepsis such as cold, blotchy or blue-tinged skin, fast breathing or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it
urgentFlags: Being unable to keep fluids down for 24 hours or more
Signs of dehydration such as dizziness, very dark urine or not peeing for 8 hours or more
Vomiting with bloody diarrhoea
Vomiting for more than 2 days
Vomiting with a weakened immune system, diabetes or kidney disease, or during pregnancy

commonCauses.title: Gastroenteritis (stomach bug)
commonCauses.detail: Often with diarrhoea; usually caused by a virus such as norovirus.

commonCauses.title: Food poisoning
commonCauses.detail: Starts within hours to days of eating contaminated food.

commonCauses.title: Alcohol or medicines
commonCauses.detail: Drinking too much or side effects of some medicines.

commonCauses.title: Migraine or motion sickness
commonCauses.detail: Vomiting can accompany a migraine or travel sickness.

commonCauses.title: Pregnancy
commonCauses.detail: Vomiting is common in early pregnancy.

selfCare: Stay at home and rest
Take small, frequent sips of water; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy can help replace lost salts
Eat when you feel able, starting with plain foods
Wash your hands often and clean surfaces to avoid spreading a stomach bug
Stay off work or school until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea
avoid: Fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse
Preparing food for others while unwell
Alcohol
seeDoctorIf: Vomiting keeps coming back over several weeks
You have lost weight without trying
You think a medicine is causing it

name: Vomiting in babies and children
summary: Vomiting in children is usually caused by a stomach bug and stops within 1 to 2 days. The main risk is dehydration, especially in babies.
redFlags: Green or yellow-green vomit, or vomit with blood or that looks like coffee grounds
Floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake
A stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, or a bulging soft spot
Severe tummy pain or a swollen, hard tummy
Signs of severe dehydration such as no wet nappies or not peeing all day, cold hands and feet, or sunken eyes
urgentFlags: A baby under 1 who will not take feeds or keeps vomiting feeds
Signs of dehydration such as fewer wet nappies, a dry mouth or no tears
Vomiting for more than 2 days, or with diarrhoea for more than 2 days in a child under 5
Forceful (projectile) vomiting after every feed in a baby under 2 months
Vomiting after a head injury
Vomiting in a child with diabetes

commonCauses.title: Stomach bug
commonCauses.detail: Gastroenteritis, usually with diarrhoea, is the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Posseting and reflux
commonCauses.detail: Bringing up small amounts of milk after feeds is normal in babies who are feeding and growing well.

commonCauses.title: Other infections
commonCauses.detail: Ear, throat or urine infections can make children vomit.

commonCauses.title: Pyloric stenosis or blockage
commonCauses.detail: Less common; forceful vomiting in young babies or green vomit needs urgent checking.

selfCare: Keep breast or formula feeding little and often
Give small, frequent sips of fluids; oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy helps
Offer food when your child feels able
Wash hands often and keep children off nursery or school until 48 hours after the last episode
avoid: Fruit juice or fizzy drinks
Anti-sickness or anti-diarrhoea medicines for children unless a doctor prescribes them
Diluting formula milk
seeDoctorIf: Your baby keeps bringing up feeds and is not gaining weight
Vomiting keeps coming back
You are worried about your child

name: Watery eyes
summary: Watery eyes are common and can be caused by irritation, allergies, dry eyes or blocked tear ducts. They often settle without treatment.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision
A chemical has got into the eye
An injury that has pierced or cut the eye
urgentFlags: Any change to your vision
Severe eye pain
A watery eye that is very red and painful, or sensitive to light

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes
commonCauses.detail: Irritated dry eyes can make too many reflex tears.

commonCauses.title: Allergies and conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and eye infections cause watering, itching and redness.

commonCauses.title: Blocked tear duct
commonCauses.detail: Common in babies and older adults; tears cannot drain so they spill over.

commonCauses.title: Eyelid problems
commonCauses.detail: Eyelids turning in or out, or blepharitis, can cause watering.

commonCauses.title: Irritants
commonCauses.detail: Wind, cold, smoke or a speck of dust can make eyes water.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about eye drops for dryness or allergy
Hold a warm compress over closed eyes and gently massage the eyelids
Clean crusty eyelids with cooled boiled water
Protect your eyes from wind and cold with glasses
avoid: Rubbing your eyes
Smoky environments
seeDoctorIf: Your eyes keep watering and it is affecting everyday activities
Your eyelid is turning inwards or drooping away from the eye
You have lumps or swelling around the eyes that have not improved

name: Wheezing
summary: Wheezing is a whistling sound when you breathe, caused by narrowed airways. It is common with asthma and chest infections, and new or worsening wheezing should be checked.
redFlags: Severe breathlessness, unable to speak, eat or sleep
Lips or skin turning blue, grey or very pale
Reliever inhaler is not helping, or you need it more than every 4 hours
Wheezing with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat after eating, a sting or a medicine
Feeling drowsy, confused or exhausted from breathing
urgentFlags: Wheezing for the first time
Asthma symptoms getting worse, or needing your reliever more often than usual
Wheezing with a high temperature or chest pain

commonCauses.title: Asthma
commonCauses.detail: Airways become narrow and inflamed, often triggered by colds, allergens, exercise or cold air.

commonCauses.title: Chest infections
commonCauses.detail: Bronchitis and, in young children, bronchiolitis can cause wheezing.

commonCauses.title: COPD
commonCauses.detail: Long-term lung damage, usually from smoking.

commonCauses.title: Allergic reaction
commonCauses.detail: Sudden wheezing can be part of anaphylaxis.

commonCauses.title: Heart failure or acid reflux
commonCauses.detail: Less common causes of wheezing.

selfCare: If you have asthma, follow your personal asthma action plan and use your reliever inhaler as prescribed
Sit upright and try to breathe slowly
Avoid known triggers such as smoke, dust and pollen
Stop smoking
avoid: Smoking and second-hand smoke
Relying on your reliever inhaler without telling a doctor it is needed more often
Exercising hard while wheezy
seeDoctorIf: You have wheezing that has not been diagnosed
Your asthma is waking you at night or you use your reliever 3 or more times a week
Wheezing keeps coming back with colds

name: White patches in the mouth or oral thrush
summary: White patches in the mouth are often caused by oral thrush, a fungal infection that is easily treated. White patches that cannot be wiped off and do not go away should be checked by a dentist or doctor.
redFlags: Difficulty breathing or swallowing with mouth swelling
urgentFlags: Pain or difficulty when swallowing
A baby with thrush who is not feeding well
Thrush in someone with a weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Oral thrush
commonCauses.detail: Creamy white patches that may wipe off, leaving red areas; more common with antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures or diabetes.

commonCauses.title: Coated tongue
commonCauses.detail: A harmless white coating from dead cells and bacteria, often with a dry mouth.

commonCauses.title: Lichen planus
commonCauses.detail: Lacy white patches on the inside of the cheeks or tongue.

commonCauses.title: Leukoplakia
commonCauses.detail: White patches that do not rub off; can occasionally become cancerous, so it needs checking.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about antifungal treatment for oral thrush
Rinse your mouth after using a steroid inhaler
Clean dentures every day and take them out at night
Brush your teeth and gently brush your tongue twice a day
avoid: Smoking
Sugary foods and mouthwashes containing alcohol while you have thrush
seeDoctorIf: Thrush has not improved after 1 week of treatment
White patches cannot be wiped off or keep coming back
A baby under 4 months has signs of thrush
White or red patches have lasted more than 3 weeks

name: Wisdom tooth pain
aliases: swollen gum at back of mouth
summary: Wisdom teeth come through at the back of the mouth in late teens or adulthood. When there is not enough space, the gum over them can become sore, swollen or infected.
redFlags: Swelling in the mouth or neck making it difficult to breathe, swallow or speak
Swelling spreading towards the eye or down the neck
Unable to open the mouth with fever and feeling very unwell
urgentFlags: A swollen cheek or jaw
A high temperature with pain at the back of the mouth
Pus or a bad taste from the gum, with pain
Severe pain that painkillers do not control

commonCauses.title: Erupting wisdom tooth
commonCauses.detail: Pain and tenderness as the tooth breaks through.

commonCauses.title: Pericoronitis
commonCauses.detail: Infection of the gum flap over a partly erupted tooth, where food gets trapped.

commonCauses.title: Decay or gum disease
commonCauses.detail: Wisdom teeth are hard to clean, so they decay more easily.

selfCare: Rinse with warm salt water (adults only), especially after eating
Brush carefully around the area with a soft toothbrush
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Eat soft foods and chew on the other side
avoid: Leaving food trapped around the tooth
Smoking
Assuming the pain will settle if it keeps coming back
seeDoctorIf: Pain lasts more than 2 or 3 days
Pain keeps coming back
You find it hard to clean around the tooth

name: Worries about eating, weight or body shape
summary: Spending a lot of time worrying about weight, food or body shape, restricting food, bingeing or making yourself sick can be signs of an eating disorder. These are serious but treatable, and early help makes a difference.
redFlags: Fainting, chest pain, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or confusion
Vomiting blood, or severe weakness after repeated vomiting
Thoughts of suicide or harming yourself
urgentFlags: Rapid weight loss or being unable to eat or drink
Feeling dizzy, very cold or very weak
Making yourself sick or using laxatives several times a day

commonCauses.title: Anorexia, bulimia and binge eating disorder
commonCauses.detail: The main types of eating disorder; they can affect anyone of any age, gender or size.

commonCauses.title: Stress and low self-esteem
commonCauses.detail: Controlling food can become a way to cope.

commonCauses.title: Social and family pressures
commonCauses.detail: Pressure about appearance, dieting culture or certain sports.

commonCauses.title: Other mental health conditions
commonCauses.detail: Anxiety, depression and OCD often occur alongside.

selfCare: Talk to someone you trust about your worries
Contact an eating disorder support line or service for advice
Try to eat regular meals rather than skipping meals or strict dieting
Unfollow social media accounts that make you feel worse about your body
avoid: Extreme diets, fasting or diet pills
Weighing yourself many times a day
Pro-eating disorder websites and communities
seeDoctorIf: Food, weight or body shape is taking over your thoughts
You are restricting, bingeing or purging
Someone close to you is worried about your eating
Your periods have stopped or you have lost a lot of weight

name: Yellow skin in a newborn
summary: Jaundice is common in newborn babies and usually harmless, fading within 2 weeks. Some babies need checks or treatment, so tell your midwife, health visitor or doctor if you notice it.
redFlags: Your baby is floppy, very drowsy, hard to wake or not feeding
A seizure (fit), arching of the back or a high-pitched cry
A temperature of 38C (100.4F) or higher
urgentFlags: Jaundice that starts in the first 24 hours after birth
Pale, chalky-coloured poo or dark yellow pee
Jaundice getting deeper or spreading, or your baby is sleepy and not feeding well
Jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks (3 weeks if born early)

commonCauses.title: Physiological jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Very common; the baby's liver is still developing and it usually clears within 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Breast milk jaundice
commonCauses.detail: Can last longer in breastfed babies and is usually harmless.

commonCauses.title: Blood group differences or infection
commonCauses.detail: Can cause jaundice in the first 24 hours.

commonCauses.title: Liver problems
commonCauses.detail: Rare; pale poo and dark pee need urgent checking.

selfCare: Tell your midwife, health visitor or doctor if you think your baby looks yellow
Feed your baby often, at least 8 to 12 times a day in the first days
Check the colour of your baby's poo and pee
Check for yellowing in the whites of the eyes, gums or palms, especially on darker skin
avoid: Putting your baby in direct sunlight to treat jaundice
Giving water or glucose water instead of milk
seeDoctorIf: You notice any yellowing of your baby's skin or eyes
Your baby's poo is pale or pee is dark
You are worried about how much your baby is feeding

name: Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)
summary: Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes is called jaundice and can be a sign of a problem with the liver, gallbladder or pancreas. It always needs to be checked by a doctor.
redFlags: Jaundice with confusion, extreme drowsiness or vomiting blood
Jaundice with severe stomach pain and a high temperature or shivering
urgentFlags: Any new yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Jaundice with dark pee, pale poo or itchy skin
Jaundice in a newborn baby that starts in the first 24 hours or lasts more than 2 weeks

commonCauses.title: Gallstones
commonCauses.detail: A stone blocking the bile duct, often with pain under the right ribs.

commonCauses.title: Hepatitis
commonCauses.detail: Liver inflammation from viruses, alcohol or medicines.

commonCauses.title: Gilbert's syndrome
commonCauses.detail: A common, harmless condition causing mild jaundice during illness or fasting.

commonCauses.title: Pancreatic or liver cancer
commonCauses.detail: Less common; often painless jaundice with weight loss.

selfCare: Get medical advice the same day
Avoid alcohol until you have been checked
Make a list of all medicines and supplements you take
avoid: Alcohol
Herbal remedies or supplements that may affect the liver
Taking more paracetamol than the pack allows
seeDoctorIf: You have been told you have mild jaundice before and it comes back often
You have ongoing itchy skin
You are worried about your liver
